sampleAnswers.answer:
Orwell's Nineteen Eighty-Four invites us to reconsider loneliness to a considerable extent as a human experience, though not the one a reader might expect. The common understanding is that loneliness is the absence of other people. The novel complicates this by presenting a man who is most isolated when he is surrounded by others, and by suggesting that the Party has turned solitude into a political condition. Through Winston Smith's experience of the telescreen, the crowd and the Party's language, Orwell presents loneliness first as something imposed by the state, and then, at the end, as something so thoroughly absorbed that its victim no longer feels it as a loss.

The opening chapter establishes the conditions of isolation. Winston's flat is watched by a telescreen, and the poster of Big Brother insists “BIG BROTHER IS WATCHING YOU”. His only refuge is an alcove where he remains “outside the range of the telescreen”, so that he can be heard but not seen. The qualification matters. Privacy in the novel is partial concealment, not safety, because observation is unpredictable and there is “no way of knowing” when one is watched. A person who can never be sure of being unobserved cannot fully trust any relationship, so the reader meets loneliness first as permanent exposure.

Winston's diary is the clearest expression of his need for another mind. He keeps it hidden in a drawer and writes it in the alcove, addressed “to the future or to the past”. In it he imagines a time when “men are different from one another” and “do not live alone”. The phrase “from the age of solitude” names the present as an age defined by isolation, set beside Big Brother and doublethink as one of its conditions. Writing becomes a substitute for conversation, a companionship with a reader who does not yet exist. That the diary must be hidden shows how little company the Party allows even in thought.

Loneliness is also shown in the crowd. At the Two Minutes Hate, the staff of the Records Department are gathered before the telescreen, and in its second minute the Hate “rose to a frenzy”. Winston is swept up in it, yet his hatred, as the narrator puts it, can be switched “like the flame of a blowlamp” from Goldstein to Big Brother and back. The crowd's unity is manufactured, and Winston's private doubt sets him apart. His heart goes out to the “lonely, derided heretic” on the screen, the “sole guardian of truth and sanity”, and the phrase describes Winston as much as Goldstein. The crowd does not relieve his loneliness; it reveals it.

Winston's isolation is intellectual as well as emotional. He is “a lonely ghost”, uttering “a truth that nobody would ever hear”, so loneliness here is the condition of holding a truth that cannot be shared. Love offers the novel's most sustained answer, and Orwell qualifies it at every step. Julia's note reads “I LOVE YOU”, and “the desire to stay alive” rises in Winston at once. In the countryside he recognises the landscape of his recurring dream, murmuring that it is “the Golden Country—almost”. Yet the room above Mr Charrington's shop, which seems a sanctuary, proves to be a trap, and the relationship ends in fear and betrayal rather than in a new community.

The Party also makes family and friendship unsafe. Parsons, the neighbour, is arrested after his little daughter denounces him for talking in his sleep, and he speaks of her with “a sort of doleful pride”. Syme, a colleague at the Ministry, is too clever to survive, and Winston thinks that “Syme will be vaporized”. The narrator observes that “You did not have friends nowadays”, only comrades. Where closeness is a risk, companionship gives way to mutual suspicion, and loneliness becomes the ordinary condition of social life.

O'Brien's interrogation turns this reconsideration into a demonstration. He asks Winston, “Do you understand that you are ALONE?”, and tells him he is “outside history”. In the same conversation he calls him “the last man” and “the guardian of the human spirit”, and the two descriptions sit uneasily together. The Party cannot allow Winston to be a hero of solitary integrity, because even that isolation depends on a belief the Party seeks to destroy. Winston's loneliness is therefore removed rather than cured. It goes first when he offers Julia to the rats with the words “Do it to Julia!”, and then when he surrenders.

The final chapter completes the process. Winston sits in the Chestnut Tree Café, where the narrator notes “two gin-scented tears” before the sentence “He had won the victory over himself”. The narrative closes with “He loved Big Brother”. Julia, the diary and the room have been taken from him, and the emptiness is felt not as loss but as contentment. To a considerable extent, then, the novel invites reconsideration: loneliness is not only the absence of company but the loss of a shared world in which company means anything. The Party makes people lonely among others and then makes that loneliness feel like belonging. Orwell offers no consolation in love or friendship, because both are shown to be fragile, and the most complete loneliness is the inability to want anyone else.
sampleAnswers.feedback: This answer meets the 17-20 row: it evaluates the extent to which the novel reconsiders loneliness and sustains that judgement across the whole essay, supported by close references. Its strength is the argument that the crowd at the Two Minutes Hate reveals Winston's isolation rather than relieving it. The move that would lift it is to test the ending more directly against the earlier claim that love offers the novel's most sustained answer.

sampleAnswers.answer:
Nineteen Eighty-Four shows that loneliness is more than being by yourself, and this changes how a reader thinks about it. Winston Smith lives in Victory Mansions in London, and his flat has a telescreen that watches him all the time. The poster of Big Brother says “BIG BROTHER IS WATCHING YOU”, so even at home Winston is never fully alone. The novel's loneliness is caused by the Party, which makes people feel watched and unable to trust anyone.

Winston keeps a secret diary, which is a way of talking to someone even though nobody is allowed to read it. He writes about a future where men are different from one another and do not live alone. This shows that he wants company, and that writing the diary is a substitute for having it. He also has a relationship with Julia. She gives him a note saying “I LOVE YOU”, and for a while this makes him feel hopeful. They meet in a room above a shop owned by Mr Charrington, but the room is not safe, and the couple are later caught.

The Two Minutes Hate shows the crowd at work. Winston shouts with the other workers at the screen and gets caught up in their anger, but in his mind he is separate from them. Loneliness is also shown through Parsons, the neighbour whose little daughter reports him, and through Syme, Winston's colleague, who is in danger because he is too clever. These characters show that friendship is not safe in this society.

In the end, O'Brien tells Winston that he is alone. He asks, “Do you understand that you are ALONE?”, and calls Winston the last man. Winston is tortured until he betrays Julia and accepts the Party. At the end of the novel he is sitting in a café and he feels content. The last line says “He loved Big Brother”, which shows that Winston has stopped feeling lonely because he no longer wants anything else.

Overall, the novel makes loneliness seem more frightening than a simple absence of company. The Party controls people's trust, so loneliness is something imposed on individuals and eventually something they stop noticing. This is why the novel changes how the reader understands loneliness.
sampleAnswers.feedback: This answer sits in the 9-12 row: it explains how the Party makes Winston lonely and covers several episodes, but it mostly retells events rather than analysing how Orwell's techniques create the sense of isolation. Its strength is the link between the diary and Winston's wish for company. The move that would lift it is to choose one episode, such as the Two Minutes Hate, and analyse how the crowd makes Winston's isolation more visible.

sampleAnswers.answer: Winston Smith is a man who works at the Ministry of Truth and lives in a flat in London. He is always being watched by the telescreen, and there is a big poster of Big Brother with the words “BIG BROTHER IS WATCHING YOU”. Winston writes a diary and he feels lonely. He wants a friend, and he gets close to Julia, who gives him a note. They have a secret relationship and meet in a room above a shop. In the end they get caught and Winston is tortured by O'Brien. Winston loves Big Brother at the end of the book. This shows that loneliness is important in the novel, because the Party makes people lonely and Winston is alone even when he is with other people. The reader can see how sad this is for him.
sampleAnswers.feedback: This answer sits in the 5-8 row: it retells the plot in order and describes Winston's loneliness without analysing how the novel represents it. Its strength is the accurate sense that Winston is isolated even among other people. The move that would lift it is to choose one scene, such as the alcove, and explain how Orwell uses its setting to show isolation.

prompts.question: To what extent does the exploration of human experience in Past the Shallows invite you to reconsider your understanding of loss?
markerNotes: The stem asks for the extent of a reconsideration, so the strongest answers state how far the novel changes the understanding of loss and what limits that change, rather than simply cataloguing the losses.
Separate the losses by kind. A death, a departure, the loss of childhood and the loss of safety are different experiences, and the best answers show how the novel makes them accumulate.
Harry's drowning is the central reference, but the strongest responses use the hospital scene to show how the loss reaches the surviving brother, rather than retelling the boat trip in order.
Evaluation needs a counter-view. An answer that argues only that loss is painful does not reach the top band unless it tests whether the father's cruelty makes these losses a special case.
commonStudentErrors: Treating loss as the death of Harry alone, and ignoring Joe's departure and the loss of childhood that Miles experiences.
Retelling the boat trip and the drowning in sequence without saying what the scene shows about loss.
Asserting that the novel changes the reader's view of loss without first stating what the usual view is.
Writing a general essay on grief that never returns to Past the Shallows or to a specific moment in it.

sampleAnswers.answer:
Favel Parrett's novel Past the Shallows invites us to reconsider loss to a considerable extent, although its extent is limited by the cruelty that shapes the brothers' lives. The usual understanding of loss is that it is a single event, a death, followed by mourning and some form of closure. The novel's exploration of human experience sets that understanding aside. It presents loss as cumulative and continuous: a mother who has died before the story begins, an older brother who leaves, a childhood taken over by work and fear, and finally the drowning of the youngest brother, Harry. The novel asks the reader to see loss as something shared unevenly within a family, and often left unmarked.

The first loss the novel registers is one that does not end the life of the person lost. Joe, the eldest of the three brothers, escapes the household and goes to live with his grandfather. He leaves Harry and Miles behind, and they cannot follow him because they are too young to leave home and so remain with their father. Joe's departure is therefore both an escape and a loss handed on to the younger boys. Parrett shows that a person can be lost while still alive, and that such an absence can weigh on those who stay in ways that a death, with its ceremonies, might not.

Miles's loss is quieter, and the novel presents it as the slow replacement of childhood by responsibility. He works on the boat with his father, an abalone fisherman who drinks heavily, and at the same time he looks after Harry. The ordinary losses of childhood, such as play and safety, are absorbed into a role no child should have to hold. Miles and Joe both love to surf, so the sea is both his pleasure and his workplace. The same water that offers him relief is where his father's trade takes place. The reconsideration here is that loss need not arrive as a single moment. It can be the gradual surrender of one life for the sake of another.

Harry's loss is of safety and of the trust a child needs from the adults around him. He is the youngest and the most vulnerable, and the father's anger is aimed at him more than at the others. Harry is afraid of the water, so the boat and the sea, the places where his father's work and his brothers' pleasure are located, are places he cannot share. He finds refuge away from the house with George Fuller, a hermit, and George's dog, Jake. The friendship matters because it shows loss being eased by people outside the family. Loss in this reading is not only what is taken away. It is also what the people who should provide care fail to give.

The central loss is Harry's drowning, and the handling of that loss is the strongest evidence for reconsideration. Miles survives the water and then learns of the death from Joe. He wakes in hospital, where Joe has come back to his bedside, and Joe tells him that Harry has drowned. Because Miles has slipped into unconsciousness before the end, the death reaches him as news rather than as an event he has witnessed. The shift from the sea to a hospital room moves the loss from action into speech, and the surviving brother's grief begins with information he cannot yet absorb.

The novel also suggests that the family cannot provide the comfort that loss usually calls for. The father is the source of the boys' fear, so the household cannot contain their grief. What remains is a small circle of people outside the father's control: the hermit and his dog, and the brothers who are left. Parrett's reconsideration here is that mourning can be carried by people who are not kin, and that the bonds of family, which are supposed to make loss bearable, can also be the source of its harshest form.

The extent of this reconsideration is limited in two ways. First, the losses are caused largely by one man's cruelty, so a reader may conclude that they belong to a specific pattern of abuse rather than to loss as a general human experience. Second, the sequence of misfortunes is intense, and the losses may accumulate faster than the reader can absorb them. These limits do not undo the reconsideration. They show that the novel's sense of loss is tied to childhood, when a child has no means of leaving, and this is the most distinctive part of its argument.

Taken together, Past the Shallows asks its reader to revise the usual idea of loss. Loss is not only a death to be mourned. It is the departure of a brother who can leave, the replacement of childhood by duty, the absence of a parent's care, and the drowning of the child who was most in need of protection. The survivor is left with the question of what it means to live on when a brother has not, and the novel's refusal to offer a comfortable answer is what makes its understanding of loss so unsettling.
sampleAnswers.feedback: This answer meets the 17-20 row: it evaluates how far the novel reconsiders loss, separating loss as a cumulative condition from loss as a single death, and it tests its own claim by considering whether the father's cruelty narrows the reading. To lift it further, the paragraph on Harry and George could test the reconsideration against one specific textual moment rather than summarising the friendship.

sampleAnswers.answer:
Past the Shallows is about three brothers who grow up with their father on the south-east coast of Tasmania. The mother has died before the story starts, so the boys are already without her. Joe is the oldest, and he escapes to live with his grandfather. That leaves Harry and Miles with their father, who is an abalone fisherman and a heavy drinker, and who is violent towards the boys. Miles has to work on the boat with him and look after Harry as well, so he is also losing his childhood. Harry is afraid of the water and makes friends with George Fuller, a hermit who has a dog called Jake. This friendship is important for Harry because he is not getting that kind of care at home.

The biggest loss in the novel is the drowning of Harry. Miles survives and ends up in hospital, and Joe comes back and tells him that Harry has drowned. This shows how upsetting the news is for Miles, because he has lost his brother and he has to live with it. It also shows that loss is not only a death, since there are other losses such as Joe leaving and Miles losing his childhood. All of these losses are connected to the family, and they show that the brothers are damaged by what happens at home.

The novel makes the reader think about loss in a different way. Usually we think loss is something that happens once, like a death, and then people get over it. In this novel the losses happen over a long time, and the family does not help the boys to deal with them. The brothers have to look after each other. George and Jake give Harry a care he does not get at home, which shows that family is not the only place where people can feel loss and be supported.

Loss is also shown as something that can come from a person rather than from an accident. The father is cruel, and this makes the boys lose their safety. The novel shows that loss can be caused by people as well as by bad luck, and this is an important point. Because the father is so cruel, the losses are not simply natural, so the reader may think the book is about abuse more than about loss in general.

Overall the novel changes how people understand loss. It shows loss as something that builds up in a family and affects the children most. Joe's leaving is a loss, and Harry's death is the biggest loss. The reader is asked to think about how the surviving brother deals with this, and the book does not give an easy answer.
sampleAnswers.feedback: This answer sits in the 9-12 row: it explains the losses across the three brothers and identifies the drowning as the central loss, but much of it retells events and the references are thin. To move up, it would need to test the idea of loss as cumulative against a specific moment, such as the hospital scene, rather than asserting that the novel changes how people understand loss.

sampleAnswers.answer: Past the Shallows is a novel about three brothers, Joe, Miles and Harry, who live with their father on the coast of Tasmania. Their mother has died, and their father is a fisherman who drinks and gets angry with them. Joe is the oldest and he leaves home to live with his grandfather. Miles is the middle brother and he has to work on the boat with his dad and look after Harry at the same time. Harry is the youngest and he is scared of the water. He makes friends with a hermit called George Fuller, who has a dog called Jake. Harry drowns and Miles survives, and in the hospital Joe tells Miles what has happened. The brothers lose a lot in the book, and this makes the reader feel sad. Loss is a big part of the novel and it makes the reader think about what the brothers have lost. Joe's leaving and Harry's death are the two losses that stand out most, and the reader is left to think about how the brothers carry them.
sampleAnswers.feedback: This answer sits in the 5-8 row: it retells the story in order with a short description of each brother, and it makes almost no textual reference. The lift would come from choosing one loss, such as Joe's departure, and explaining what the novel does to make that loss feel like a loss rather than a plot event.

prompts.question: To what extent does the exploration of human experience in Dobson’s poetry invite you to reconsider your understanding of ageing?
markerNotes: The strongest answers treat 'extent' in the question as a real judgement: they say how far the poems reconsider ageing and where that reconsideration stops.
Over the Hill and Amy Caroline carry most of the argument. An answer that grounds its claims in one older figure's calm or one woman's twilight hour will outscore a survey of all seven poems.
Summer's End rewards attention to its structure. The pairing of a present and a past part is evidence of how Dobson represents time, and the top answers use it rather than summarising the poem.
Young Girl at a Window gives a useful counterweight. A student who sees change beginning in youth, not at the end of life, has a stronger case for reconsidering ageing as continuous.
commonStudentErrors: Treating ageing as only decline and answering that Dobson's older figures are sad, without testing the question's invitation to reconsider.
Describing Amy Caroline's hardship without analysing the late turn to her own music, so the poem is retold rather than evaluated.
Making claims about Dobson's biography, such as dates or family, that the poems themselves do not support.
Presenting remembered lines as exact quotations when the wording has not been checked against the book.

sampleAnswers.answer:
Dobson's poetry does invite a reconsideration of ageing, though not in the direction a reader might first expect. Her older figures are seldom pitiable and seldom wise in the stock way. Because her poems treat a life as continuous across time, the exploration of human experience is most convincing when it presents ageing as something that carries earlier selves forward rather than ending them. Over the Hill, Amy Caroline and Summer's End make this case most clearly, and Young Girl at a Window, set at the threshold of adulthood, shows how early the question of change begins. Together they suggest that ageing is marked by composure, by a return to what was loved in youth, and by a loss that is accepted rather than resisted. The invitation is substantial, but it is limited by the regret these poems refuse to hide.

Over the Hill is built around an old man close to death, and its most important choice is what it withholds. The reader expects fear, and the poem does not supply it. Dobson gives him a calm, almost cheerful self-possession, a man who handles the obstacles of his life rather than fighting them. The western light and the evening sky shape the tone: the light is not a sign of decline but of an unhurried completion. The setting also matters, since the hills and sky frame him against something larger than his own fear. This challenges the assumption that age must be a time of dread. The reconsideration is not complete, however. The calm is presented as something a man has earned through a long life of difficulty, not as a condition that arrives with age, so the poem asks the reader to reconsider old age as achievement rather than as a natural state of peace.

Amy Caroline turns the same reconsideration toward an older woman, and here the poem's sympathy is sharper. Dobson sets out a life given to a large family on very little money, summed up in the phrase “little money, many griefs”. Yet the emotional centre is a late hour. At twilight the woman sits at the piano in the semi-dark and plays “the songs learnt long ago”. The twilight becomes a private time, a return to the girl she once was, and it reconsiders the older woman as someone with an inner life that the demands of a household have not extinguished. The poem does not let this return become a simple consolation. The jinker and horse she never had stand as a small, unrealised wish, and the poem's sorrow is registered rather than explained away. Ageing, in this poem, is a return that is also an accounting of what was given up.

Summer's End uses structure to complicate ageing. The poem is a diptych, with a second part called Picnic set against the first, and the pairing lets time move in two directions. The first part turns towards the end of a season, and its opening words, “After the summer season”, set a mood of a life that has turned. The second part is more intimate. A speaker by the fire looks back, and memory brings a child running back through time to a picnic. The fire, the picnic and the child form a chain of images that moves the reader backwards, and the split between the two parts is itself a feature that carries the emotion. Ageing here is not only loss. The speaker can see her earlier self as clearly as the present, and the structure asks the reader to hold both at once.

Young Girl at a Window reverses the perspective. A girl stands at a window on the threshold between girlhood and womanhood, and the poem makes time visible in the room, in the clock whose minute hand is still and in the landscape of turning hills. Because the poem looks forward, it shows that the experience of change does not begin in old age. It is the condition of the whole life, and this is the strongest reason to reconsider ageing as continuous. The poem's reach is also limited. It speaks of the girl's uncertainty rather than of any settled wisdom, so the older figures in Dobson's collection must supply the composure that the girl has not yet found.

Dobson's poetry therefore invites a substantial reconsideration of ageing, moving the reader from an expectation of dread towards composure, return and an interior life. Over the Hill and Amy Caroline show age as a settled mind and a private hour, Summer's End holds the past beside the present, and Young Girl at a Window shows change present from the beginning. The extent is not total. These poems do not dissolve the cost of a life: Amy Caroline's sorrow and her unlived wish, and the girl's anxiety at the window, remain in view. The older lives they present are neither decline nor consolation, and that is why the reconsideration they invite is persuasive.
sampleAnswers.feedback: This answer meets the 17-20 row: it evaluates how far Dobson's older figures invite a reconsideration of ageing, and it sustains that judgement across the poems through specific images such as the western light and the twilight piano. The strongest move is the closing claim that the reconsideration is real but limited by regret. To lift it, the final paragraph could test the reconsideration more directly against the question's word 'extent', for example by naming one poem that resists the reading.

sampleAnswers.answer:
Dobson's poems show that ageing is not only decline. In Over the Hill, an old man is close to death but he is not frightened, and this makes the reader think differently about old age. He seems calm and at peace with his life, so the poem suggests that an older person can face the end without fear. This changes the idea that old age is simply sad, because the poem presents the old man as settled rather than defeated. The poem's language is direct, so its message is easy to follow.

Amy Caroline is another poem about an older woman. She raised a large family with very little money and had many difficulties in her life. At the end of the poem she sits at the piano and plays songs she learnt long ago, and this shows that she still has something that belongs to her. It means that getting older does not remove the person she used to be. The reader can therefore see the older woman as a whole person with a past, and not only as someone who worked for others. The reader also sees that she worked hard for the family, which makes her later hour at the piano seem earned.

Summer's End is about the end of summer, which can stand for getting older. The poem has two parts, and the second part has a child running back to a picnic. This shows that memories from childhood come back to the speaker, so the older speaker still remembers being young. The fire is a warm image, and it shows that the speaker is comfortable with her memories. The poem makes the reader think that ageing involves looking back as well as moving forward, which is an important idea in Dobson's work. Summer's End is about the end of summer, and the reader feels the cold coming on.

Young Girl at a Window is about a girl who is growing up and is nervous about the future. She stands at a window, which is a place between inside and outside, so the reader sees her as someone about to leave home. The poem asks the reader to think about the future, so its tone is forward-looking. This shows that change starts early in life, so ageing is part of a longer process rather than a sudden end. The poem therefore supports the idea that the reader should reconsider ageing as something that begins in youth.

Overall, Dobson's poems do make the reader reconsider ageing to some extent, because they show calm, memory and an inner life. However, the poems also show that older people carry regret and sorrow, so the reconsideration is not complete.
sampleAnswers.feedback: This answer sits in the 9-12 row: it explains how Dobson's older figures challenge the idea that ageing is only decline, but its references are thin and it retells the poems rather than analysing how the poetic features create the reconsideration. The strongest move is the link between the second part of Summer's End and the speaker's memory. To lift it, choose one feature of Amy Caroline, such as the twilight setting, and explain what it changes about the reader's view of the woman.

sampleAnswers.answer: Dobson writes about older people in Over the Hill and Amy Caroline. In Over the Hill an old man is near death and he is calm. He does not seem scared, which shows that old age can be peaceful. There is a sunset in the poem, and the light makes the scene look quiet. Amy Caroline is about an older woman who had lots of children and not much money. She plays the piano at dusk and remembers old songs. The poem makes clear that her life was full of work for other people, and the reader feels sorry for her. The poem shows that she still enjoys things for herself. So the poems show that older people still have things they enjoy, and the reader can think about ageing in a different way. Dobson shows that growing old is not always sad. The poem about the girl at the window is also about change, and the girl is nervous about growing up, so the reader can see that getting older happens at every age.
sampleAnswers.feedback: This answer sits in the 5-8 row: it describes Over the Hill and Amy Caroline and makes a general claim about ageing, with minimal textual reference and little analysis of how the poetry produces the effect. Its strength is the basic point that the older figures are calm rather than sad. To lift it, quote one specific image from each poem and say what it shows about the older person.

prompts.question: To what extent does the exploration of human experience in Slessor’s poetry invite you to reconsider your understanding of struggle?
markerNotes: The strongest answers do not treat struggle as one thing. They separate the collective endurance of Beach Burial, the daily survival in William Street and the losing contest with Time in Out of Time, and then ask which of these the reader is most moved to reconsider.

An answer that argues the extent claim should test it against the poems' limits. Slessor's speakers often watch suffering rather than share it, and a sharp answer turns that observation into an argument rather than a complaint.

Close reference to one word or one image does more than a paragraph of plot. The contrast between the lovely and the ugly in William Street, and the trousers hanging in the window, carry more analysis than a summary of what the street contains.
Context about the Depression should be used selectively. One clause linking the pawned trousers to unemployment does more work than a background paragraph on the economy.
commonStudentErrors: Treating the three poems as a survey of war and poverty, rather than arguing about how far they change the reader's understanding of struggle.
Retelling the poems in order without showing how the language of each one produces a changed view of struggle.
Presenting the burial on the beach as a heroic battle, when the poem focuses on the nameless dead and the soldiers' quiet labour.
Assuming Slessor's sympathy for the poor is uncritical, and not testing whether the poems also admire the scenes they describe.

sampleAnswers.answer:
Kenneth Slessor’s exploration of human experience invites a reconsideration of struggle to a considerable extent, though not in the way a reader might first expect. Much writing about hardship locates struggle in heroic action, a battle to win or a cause to defend. Slessor finds it instead in the endurance of people who never chose their conflict and are rarely named. Beach Burial, William Street and Out of Time show three distinct kinds of struggle: the grim labour of burying the unidentified dead, the daily survival of the poor on a city street, and a speaker’s losing contest with Time itself. Read together, these poems suggest that struggle is less a single event than a condition, and that its meaning depends on whom the poem chooses to look at.

In Beach Burial the struggle is collective and almost wordless. The dead are seamen pulled from the surf, and the men who bury them are battle-hardened troops whose rites are rough but tender. Each grave carries a cross inscribed “Unknown Seaman”, and those two words hold the poem’s central tension: the sailors have lost their lives and their names, yet they still receive a burial. The struggle here does not belong to the fight that killed them. It belongs to the living, who must bury strangers and feel something for them with no reward. The poem’s tone is one of perplexity rather than assertion, and that uncertainty invites a reader to reconsider war as something whose costs continue after the battle ends. A reader who expects heroism finds instead a quiet, unglamorous labour, and the poem treats that labour as a form of endurance.

William Street reconsiders struggle through people the city has discarded. The poem’s four quatrains move through a rainy night on a Sydney street that, in the 1930s, was known for poverty, crime and prostitution. The speaker finds the scene “lovely”, and a refrain sets this against an unnamed “you” who finds it “ugly”. The contrast forces a reader to ask whether ugliness belongs to the suffering itself or only to the comfortable observer who looks away. Pawnshop trousers hang in the windows like hanged men, a grim image that suggests unemployed men who have pawned what they owned to survive the Depression. The poem then turns to the figures on the pavement, who are close to starvation, and gives them a dignity that respectable society refuses. Here struggle is undramatic. It is the work of getting through a night, and the poem makes that work visible without making it heroic.

Out of Time turns the struggle inward and makes its adversary Time. The opening line, “I saw Time flowing like the hundred yachts”, presents time as a procession that the speaker watches and is then swept into, rather than as a clock to be read. The imagery is bright, with light cutting under the harbour and sails moving in daylight, and the speaker is absorbed in the moment. The poem then describes Time as an assault that takes hold of him, and the brightness darkens. The yachts become a funeral procession, the gulls fall and the body decays. The struggle is a losing one, and the poem treats it as a permanent condition of being alive. The poem’s one counterweight is a brief vision that seems to pause ordinary time, which is what the title names. This recasts endurance as the effort to hold a moment before it passes, a struggle that is a matter of perception rather than victory.

These poems do not invite reconsideration without limit, however. Each struggle is seen from outside. The speaker of William Street watches the street rather than entering the lives of the men whose trousers hang in the window, and the sailors of Beach Burial are nameless, so their suffering is known only through the people who bury them. Slessor’s sympathy is real, but the poetry sometimes admires a scene as much as it asks why the scene exists. A reader can end the poem moved by the beauty of its images without asking what might change the conditions behind them. The poems therefore change what counts as struggle, but they leave open whether such suffering is the price of city and war life or something that could be ended.

Overall, Slessor’s poetry reconsiders struggle to a considerable extent. It moves the idea away from campaigns and battles towards the burden of the unnamed dead, the endurance of the poor on a city street and the mind’s losing contest with time. The reconsideration is strongest where the poems unsettle a reader’s own judgement, as the refrain of William Street does. Struggle, in these poems, is not always heroic and not always won. It is what human beings keep doing when no outcome is promised, and Slessor asks his reader to notice it rather than look away.
sampleAnswers.feedback: This answer meets the 17-20 row: it assesses the extent of the reconsideration, sustains a clear judgement across three prescribed poems, and supports each point with close references. Its strongest move is reading the lovely and ugly refrain of William Street as a test of the reader's own judgement. The one move left is to examine the limits of its argument with the same precision it gives the poems' strengths.

sampleAnswers.answer:
Slessor’s poems make a reader think harder about struggle. In Beach Burial, soldiers bury sailors who have been pulled out of the surf onto a beach. The soldiers are doing a hard job and it makes them feel sad. The crosses say “Unknown Seaman”, which shows that the men died without names, and this makes the reader feel sorry for them. The poem makes us think about war in a new way, because war is not only about fighting. It is also about the people who are left to deal with the dead, and that is a kind of struggle too. Those who are left have to keep going after the fighting has stopped. The poem shows that the burial is a hard thing to do and that the men doing it are affected by it, so the reader can see that struggle continues after a battle is over.

William Street is about a street in Sydney at night. It is rough and full of poor people, and the speaker thinks it is lovely even though someone else thinks it is “ugly”. This shows that people can see the same place in different ways. The poem has a lot of different things in it, like lights, smells and people walking around. The poem also has trousers in a pawnshop window, which suggests the men who owned them have lost their jobs and their money. That is a struggle, because they cannot afford clothes or food. The poem repeats the same idea in each stanza, which makes the reader think about it more. The reader can see that these people are struggling to survive in the city, and that is what the poem is about, so it makes us reconsider how we think about poor people.

Out of Time is about Time, which the speaker describes as a procession of yachts. He is caught up in the moment at first, and the images are bright and full of light. Then the poem gets darker and the yachts become a funeral, so the poem moves towards death. The poem also seems to say that people cannot stop time from passing. This shows that time is a struggle for everyone and the speaker cannot win against it. So the poem changes the idea of struggle, because struggle is not something you can win but something that goes on anyway. The change in mood from bright to dark shows the reader how the speaker feels about losing.

Overall, the poems make me reconsider struggle because they show it in ordinary people rather than heroes. They show that struggle happens in war and in the city, and also against time. The poems show a lot of different things, and I think they invite a reconsideration of struggle, although some poems do this better than others. Beach Burial is probably the most moving, and William Street is probably the most interesting because it has the lovely and ugly contrast in it.
sampleAnswers.feedback: This answer sits in the 9-12 row: it explains what happens in each poem and reaches a general view, but it rarely analyses how the language produces that view. Its strength is the attention to the poems' sympathy for ordinary people. The move that would lift it is to choose one technique in each poem and show what it does to the reader's view of struggle.

sampleAnswers.answer: Slessor writes about struggle in his poems. In Beach Burial, some sailors have died in the sea and the soldiers bury them on a beach. The men are dead and they are washed up from the water, and the soldiers have to dig graves in the sand. There are crosses with the words “Unknown Seaman”, so the men did not have names. That shows the men were not known to anyone. In William Street there is a street in Sydney at night with lights and smells and poor people. The speaker says it is “lovely” but someone else says it is “ugly”. The street is busy and has lots of different people on it. In Out of Time, the speaker sees time like boats going past and then it gets sad. Time is a struggle because it keeps going and you cannot stop it. Struggle is in all of the poems because people have problems. So the poems show that struggle is a big idea and Slessor thinks about it a lot.
sampleAnswers.feedback: This answer sits in the 5-8 row: it describes the poems and retells their settings, with only one textual reference. Its strength is that it notices the contrast between lovely and ugly in William Street. The move that would lift it is to explain what the poem does with that contrast rather than repeating what it says.

prompts.question: To what extent does the exploration of human experience in Rainbow’s End invite you to reconsider your understanding of acceptance?
markerNotes: The question turns on acceptance, so the strongest answers show that the play gives the word more than one meaning: Nan Dear’s caution, Gladys’s demand for entitlements, and the test a romance across the colour line puts on personal goodwill.

Gladys is the most useful figure for a reconsideration argument, because her campaign presents acceptance as something demanded rather than granted. An answer that analyses how she makes her case, not only what she wants, moves into the top rows.

Keep the institutional and the personal apart. An answer that separates officials who obstruct the family from individuals who show goodwill has a more precise account of acceptance than one that treats prejudice as a single force.

The question asks to what extent, so the answer must commit to a degree and argue for its limits. The strongest responses say where the play stops short of a full reconsideration, and why, rather than ending on a general statement about tolerance.
commonStudentErrors: Treating acceptance as general tolerance or kindness, without connecting it to housing, schooling and power in the play.
Presenting Nan Dear as old-fashioned or wrong, and so missing why her caution is a serious position the play takes seriously.
Retelling who the characters are and what Gladys wants, without asking how their conflicts change the audience’s idea of acceptance.
Reading the romance between Dolly and Errol as a love story alone, rather than as a test of whether personal goodwill matches community acceptance.

sampleAnswers.answer:
Jane Harrison’s Rainbow’s End is set in regional Victoria in the 1950s, in a shanty on the flats of the Goulburn River, and its three generations of Aboriginal women live in a community where every improvement depends on people who hold power over them. Read through that setting, the play’s exploration of human experience invites you to reconsider your understanding of acceptance, and the play makes a strong case for doing so. The usual understanding treats acceptance as something a minority earns by fitting in, keeping quiet and avoiding trouble. Harrison shows acceptance instead as a question of power: who is allowed a proper home, an education and a place in the town, and who must wait to be let in. The reconsideration is not total, because the play takes seriously the caution that keeps a family safe, but the idea of acceptance most audiences bring to the play is shown to be inadequate.

The argument begins with Nan Dear, the grandmother, whose view of acceptance is the most conventional and the most hard-won. Nan is wary of change and wants the family to stay out of sight, and her advice reads as a lifetime’s judgement about how far a family can push before it loses what little it has. A reader might expect the play to make her a figure of defeat. The more demanding reading is that Harrison gives her caution real weight, so the audience must set it against the cost of living below the town’s notice. Nan is irascible rather than foolish, and her position forces the question of whether acceptance that depends on silence is acceptance at all.

Gladys stands at the other pole. She campaigns for better housing for her community, and she has little formal schooling, so her case is built from experience and persistence rather than from the education the officials recognise. The women voice their need for housing in public, and that speaking is itself a refusal of the older idea of acceptance. For Gladys, acceptance is not a feeling the wider community might offer once it is ready. It is a set of entitlements: a proper home, steady work and a daughter with a real chance in life. Her campaign reconsiders acceptance as recognition, something a community demands from the state and the town rather than something it waits to be granted. Her limited schooling sharpens the point, because the people refused acceptance are also those the system has denied the tools to argue for it.

The romance between Dolly and Errol tests acceptance at its most personal point. Dolly is bright and witty, and she dreams of becoming a nurse, which gives her a future her grandmother can barely picture. Errol is a young white salesman who falls for her, and the relationship across the colour line raises a question the older women cannot avoid: whether the wider community will accept a young Aboriginal woman as an equal partner. The question also exposes a distinction the play makes available. Errol’s regard for Dolly is one kind of acceptance, the town’s treatment of the family is another, and an individual’s goodwill can sit alongside a community that still refuses the family. The romance is therefore not a side plot. It is the place where the abstract idea of acceptance becomes uncomfortably personal.

The institutional side of the play is where acceptance is most plainly withheld. Officials and government representatives obstruct the family’s efforts, so the women are not failing to be accepted because they are too loud or too quiet. The obstacle is structural: the housing and schooling systems do not extend to Aboriginal families the same rights they extend to white ones. This is the strongest reason to reconsider the idea that acceptance is a matter of personal attitude. If individuals are kind to a family but the institutions still exclude it, then acceptance has been reduced to a private courtesy. The play implies that it should be a condition of citizenship, and that the women’s campaign is an attempt to make it so.

To what extent, then, does Rainbow’s End invite a reconsideration of acceptance? To a considerable extent. The play separates three things audiences tend to run together: the private tolerance of individuals, the quiet survival strategy of a family, and the public recognition a community is owed. Nan Dear’s caution, Gladys’s campaign and Dolly’s relationship with Errol each sit at a different point along that line, and the play does not rank them simply. What it does make clear is that acceptance which depends on a family’s silence, or on the goodwill of one outsider, falls short of the full acceptance a community is entitled to. The reconsideration is therefore not a rejection of Nan’s wisdom but a widening of what acceptance must include.
sampleAnswers.feedback: This answer meets the 17-20 row: it sustains a thesis that acceptance is shaped by power, and it sets Nan Dear’s caution against Gladys’s campaign and the romance with Errol so the argument moves with the question. The move that would lift it is to anchor the Dolly and Errol section in one exact moment from the play, so the reference is closer to the text and less to the plot in general.

sampleAnswers.answer:
Rainbow’s End is about human experience under pressure, and it asks whether the audience’s idea of acceptance is good enough. The play is set in a shanty on the Goulburn River flats in regional Victoria in the 1950s, where three generations of women live together. Nan Dear, the grandmother, wants the family to stay out of sight. Gladys, her daughter, wants a proper home and steady work, and she campaigns for better housing. Dolly, Gladys’s daughter, wants to be a nurse. Errol is a young salesman who falls in love with Dolly, and this causes problems because of the colour line. These characters are the way the play raises questions about acceptance.

The play does invite the audience to reconsider acceptance to some extent. Acceptance can mean fitting in and not causing trouble, and Nan thinks this is how a family survives. Gladys does not agree with her. She speaks up for housing, which shows that the family wants more than to be tolerated. The women voicing their need for better housing is a clear example of the play challenging the older idea. Their struggle is about getting the same things other people get, such as a decent house and a chance at an education, so acceptance here means equal treatment.

The romance between Dolly and Errol also makes the audience think about acceptance. The relationship is a problem for the wider community, and it shows that individual acceptance is different from community acceptance. Dolly is bright and has a plan for her life, so her story is about her own future as well as about the relationship. This matters because it means acceptance is not only about what other people think of her, and the play shows her wanting more than their approval.

The officials in the play are another reason acceptance is difficult. They obstruct the family, so the women cannot simply be accepted by keeping quiet. This means acceptance is not only a personal matter but also a matter of who has power. The play shows the family having to fight for what they need, and this fight is what makes the audience see acceptance differently from the way Nan does.

Overall, the play invites the audience to reconsider acceptance because it connects acceptance to housing, education and power. Nan’s view is understandable, but Gladys and Dolly show other possibilities. The audience is left to think about whether acceptance is something people wait for or something they demand. The play also shows that the individual and the community do not always agree about who belongs.
sampleAnswers.feedback: This answer sits in the 9-12 row: it explains how acceptance connects to housing, education and power, but it retells who the characters are and offers few textual references, so the analysis stays general. The move that would lift it is to choose one exchange between Nan and Gladys and show how their disagreement changes what the audience understands about acceptance.

sampleAnswers.answer: Rainbow’s End is a play about three Aboriginal women in the 1950s. Nan Dear is the grandmother and she does not like change. She wants the family to keep quiet. Gladys is her daughter and she wants a better house and a better job. She fights for housing for the community. Dolly is the young one and she wants to be a nurse. Dolly has a relationship with Errol, who is a salesman. The play shows that it is hard for them to be accepted by the town. Acceptance is important, and everyone should be treated the same. Nan and Gladys have different ideas about what the family should do. Harrison uses the family to show what it feels like to be treated unfairly, and the audience can see the problems the family has with the government and the town.
sampleAnswers.feedback: This answer sits in the 5-8 row: it describes the family and the situation with almost no textual reference, and it states a view of acceptance rather than analysing how the play presents it. The move that would lift it is to choose one character and explain how the play makes that character’s idea of acceptance visible.

prompts.question: To what extent does the exploration of human experience in The Crucible invite you to reconsider your understanding of love?
markerNotes: The strongest answers take 'to what extent' seriously: they say how far the play reconsiders love and where it stops, rather than announcing that it does.
Abigail is the easiest relationship to write about and the one that most often produces retelling. The stronger answer asks what her desire does to the other characters, not only what she does.
The Act Four exchange between Elizabeth and John is where the reconsideration is clearest. Close reference to Elizabeth's own words there does more work than another summary of the court scenes.
Do not treat Elizabeth's lie in Act Three as only a betrayal or only an act of love. The best answers hold both readings and explain which one the play allows.
commonStudentErrors: Calling the Proctors' marriage simply a romance without addressing the affair that breaks its trust.
Treating Abigail's feelings as ordinary love rather than a possessive desire that turns into accusation.
Retelling the trials in order without saying what any scene shows about love.
Presenting Elizabeth's Act Four forgiveness as a happy ending, when John still cannot forgive himself.

sampleAnswers.answer:
To a considerable extent, The Crucible invites its audience to reconsider love, though not in the romantic sense the word usually carries. Arthur Miller sets the play in Salem in 1692, and the human experience it explores is shaped by suspicion, reputation and the demand for public confession. In that climate love is shown to be possessive, damaged and, at its best, a moral commitment rather than a feeling. The play does not reject love. It tests love against a community that has already decided who is good and who is evil, and the result is a view of love that is harder and more demanding than the one most readers bring to it.

The first challenge to a sentimental view of love is Abigail Williams. Abigail once served in the Proctor household, and the first act reveals that she and John Proctor had an affair, for which she was dismissed. She still believes their feelings are mutual, and when she presses him, Proctor refuses in almost brutal terms: he will "cut off my hand" before he reaches for her again. Abigail's desire does not fade under rejection. It becomes jealousy, and jealousy becomes accusation. The girls' attempted curse is aimed at Elizabeth Proctor, and Abigail is willing to see Elizabeth condemned so that she can have John. Miller shows love reduced to possession, a passion that treats another person as an obstacle to be removed.

The Proctors' marriage is the play's more searching test, and Act Two shows how far it has been damaged. Proctor has lived with the affair for months, and Elizabeth has not forgiven him. He accuses her of judging him, telling her to "Learn charity, woman", and he says that "an everlasting funeral" marches round her heart. The line is cruel, but it also reveals what the marriage has become: love held in place by grief and resentment rather than by warmth. Proctor is not a neutral judge of her coldness, and the play does not let him claim the moral high ground. He has betrayed her, and he still wants her to see him as a good man.

Elizabeth's own admission in Act Four is the clearest reconsideration of love in the play. She tells John that she counted herself "so plain" and that no honest love could come to her, and she admits that her suspicion made the house cold: "It were a cold house I kept". The line turns a domestic image into an admission of her own part in the failure. It also complicates the audience's sympathy. Elizabeth has been wronged, but she has also been unable to say love, and Miller lets both truths stand.

The third act tests love in public, and here the play shows its moral complexity. Proctor confesses the affair in court to expose Abigail, and in doing so makes his private shame public knowledge. Elizabeth, questioned by Danforth, denies that there was any affair. She fears that Abigail has revealed it to ruin her husband, so she lies to protect him. Her lie is an act of loyalty, and it is also a failure of truth at the moment it matters most. Hale pleads with Danforth to reconsider, but the court holds to its judgement. For Elizabeth, love means shielding the person it loves, even at the cost of what is true.

In Act Four the theme returns with a different emphasis. Proctor signs a false confession, then refuses to hand it over and tears it up, because he does not want his family, and especially his three sons, stigmatised by a public confession. His words "Because it is my name" show that he has moved from private guilt to a defence of his public self. He has, he says, "given you my soul", and only his name is left to keep. The love the play respects here is not possessive. Elizabeth, who has been cold, recognises this when she answers Hale with "He have his goodness now", and she will not persuade him back to the lie, because "God forbid I take it from him".

Abigail, whose desire ended in accusation, escapes Salem with her uncle's savings, a last image of love as taking. Miller does not restore the Proctors to an idealised marriage, and Elizabeth's forgiveness is won through grief rather than given in joy. Yet the play does reconsider love to a real extent. It presents love as a moral obligation: to tell the truth where possible, to shield the vulnerable, and to let another person keep his integrity. That is a demanding idea. The characters who meet it, and those who fail to, make the audience question its own assumptions about what love asks of a person.
sampleAnswers.feedback: This answer meets the 17-20 row: it evaluates the extent to which the play reconsiders love, tracing Abigail's possession, the Proctors' damaged marriage and Elizabeth's forgiveness with specific references in each case. Its strength is the reading of Elizabeth's Act Three lie as both loyalty and failure, which avoids a simple verdict. To lift it, state in the final paragraph exactly where the reconsideration stops, for example by noting that the play withholds a comfortable resolution for the Proctors.

sampleAnswers.answer:
The Crucible asks its audience to think again about love, because the love in the play is not simple. Abigail Williams wants John Proctor, and when he rejects her she becomes spiteful and dangerous. She is also jealous of Elizabeth Proctor, and the girls try to curse Elizabeth. This shows that love can turn into jealousy and then into something harmful. The audience learns that Abigail's feelings are not a healthy kind of love.

John and Elizabeth have a marriage that has been damaged by his affair. In Act Two they argue, and John tells her that she must learn charity. Elizabeth is cold towards him and does not forgive him easily. She believes he still lusts after Abigail, and she tells him that he cannot redeem himself while he does. This shows that the play is not a simple love story with a happy ending. Their relationship is more realistic, and the audience can see how hurt they both are.

In Act Three John goes to court and confesses to the affair. He does this to show that Abigail is lying, but it also makes his private life public and damages his reputation. When Elizabeth is asked about the affair she says there was none. She does this to protect her husband, which is an example of love. However, she is not telling the truth, so the love is complicated, and the court does not change its decision. Elizabeth is pregnant, and Danforth has promised to spare her until the child is born, so her life is not at immediate risk.

In the last act John has to decide whether to confess. He signs a paper and then tears it up because he does not want his sons to be shamed. Hale asks her to persuade John to confess, and she refuses. She tells Hale that John has his goodness now and she will not take it from him. This suggests a different kind of love, one that accepts John's decision. Abigail's love was about getting what she wanted, but Elizabeth's love respects John's choice.

Overall, the play makes the audience think about love in a new way. It is not only romance but also loyalty, forgiveness and respect. These ideas are tested by the events of the trials, and the society around the characters makes their love harder to show. This is why the play helps the audience reconsider what love means.
sampleAnswers.feedback: This answer sits in the 9-12 row: it explains each relationship in turn and shows some understanding of the Proctors' marriage, but it mostly sequences events and offers few quotations to support its claims about love. Its strength is the reading of Elizabeth's Act Four respect as a different kind of love. To lift it, use two or three precise quotations and make each paragraph test one claim about love rather than retelling a scene.

sampleAnswers.answer: The Crucible is a play by Arthur Miller about the Salem witch trials. It is also about love. Abigail loves John Proctor and they had an affair before the play starts. Elizabeth finds out and sends Abigail away. Abigail then tells lies and accuses people of witchcraft, including Elizabeth, and the trouble spreads to other people in the village. John goes to court and tells everyone about the affair. Elizabeth lies about it to protect him. Elizabeth is pregnant, so she is spared for now. Many other people are hanged in the same trials. At the end John tears up his confession and is led away to be hanged. The love in the play is complicated, and it makes some of the characters do bad things. The audience can see that love changes over the course of the play, and that the people involved are not always honest about what they feel.
sampleAnswers.feedback: This answer sits in the 5-8 row: it retells the affair, the trials and the ending in order, and describes what happens rather than how the play represents love. Its strength is that it correctly identifies the affair as the source of the Proctors' trouble. To lift it, choose one scene, such as Elizabeth's lie in Act Three, and explain what it shows about love.

prompts.question: To what extent does the exploration of human experience in The Merchant of Venice invite you to reconsider your understanding of deception?
markerNotes: The strongest answers treat deception as a shared social practice rather than a trait of one character, and they weigh the 'to what extent' by asking where the play exposes, excuses or rewards deceit.
Bassanio's casket speech, 'The world is still deceived with ornament', is the play's own theory of deception. Answers that use it to frame the Venetian world do more than treat the caskets as plot.

Portia's disguise, the blood clause and the ring test need to be assessed, not summarised. The best answers ask whether each deception is justified, by law or by love, and whether the play endorses it.
Linking Shylock's 'Hath not a Jew eyes?' speech to 'The villainy you teach me' shows that the play makes deception reciprocal. That link is worth more than a list of the Christians' tricks.
commonStudentErrors: Treating Shylock as the only deceiver, and ignoring the 'merry sport' framing of the bond and Antonio's own self-deception about his ships.
Retelling the caskets, the disguises and the ring test in order without explaining what each one shows about deception.
Treating Portia's disguise and the blood clause as a simple victory of justice over deceit, without weighing the trick used against Shylock.
Assuming the merciful ending resolves the question, without noticing that Shylock is made to become a Christian as the price of his life.

sampleAnswers.answer:
The exploration of human experience in The Merchant of Venice invites the audience to reconsider deception, though not in the way its opening suggests. At first deceit seems the property of an outsider. Shylock presents his bond as kindness, insisting “This is kind I offer”, and he proposes the forfeit “in a merry sport”. Bassanio suspects the bond at once, while Antonio accepts it. The play then shows that its Christian characters deceive themselves, one another and the audience just as readily. How far the play asks us to reconsider deception depends on who deceives, why, and at what cost.

Bassanio names the danger in the sharpest phrase of the scene: “fair terms and a villain's mind”. Antonio dismisses the warning, certain that his ships will “come home a month before the day”. His confidence is a self-deception the audience can see coming. When Shylock justifies interest by citing Jacob's flocks, Antonio retorts, “The devil can cite Scripture for his purpose”, and then, “O, what a goodly outside falsehood hath!” These lines accuse Shylock of hiding villainy beneath religion, yet the play's Christians will later speak of mercy while attaching conditions that make it coercive.

The Belmont caskets extend this suspicion to the whole society. Bassanio, who comes after the gold and silver caskets have caught the wrong suitors, chooses the plain lead and concludes that “The world is still deceived with ornament”. He widens the claim to law and religion, where a plea “so tainted and corrupt” can be made acceptable by “a gracious voice”. In this speech deception is not a Jewish trait but a common practice of the age, and the line “The seeming truth which cunning times put on” asks which Venetian is not implicated.

Portia's disguise is the play's most deliberate deception, and the question is whether its ends excuse it. She enters the court as Balthazar, a doctor of law, while Nerissa poses as a clerk, and she wins by a technicality: the bond grants a pound of flesh but “no jot of blood”. Gratiano's cry, “O upright judge!”, voices the Christians' triumph. The audience knows Portia's identity and Shylock does not, so the trial runs on dramatic irony, and the audience is asked to admire the wit while noticing that the law turns against the man who holds it. The sentence then requires that Shylock “presently become a Christian”. The mercy the play praises is therefore conditional, and Portia's great speech, “The quality of mercy is not strain'd”, is itself delivered in disguise, which makes the praise of mercy a performance as much as an appeal.

Shylock's reply is what most directly reconsiders the question. Defending his humanity, he asks, “Hath not a Jew eyes?”, lists the senses and passions Jews share with Christians, and argues that wrong demands revenge. His climax is that “The villainy you teach me I will execute”. Deception here is taught and returned. The play does not excuse Shylock's cruelty, but a reader who condemns his bond as deceit must ask whether the Christian example he learns from is any more honest, and why the Christians' own deceits end in marriage and laughter.

Jessica's deception of her father is treated with more sympathy, which exposes a double standard in the play. Her verdict on her father's household is “Our house is hell”, and she leaves in boy's clothes, carrying away his ducats and jewels. She knows the disguise is shameful, admitting, “I am much ashamed of my exchange”. In the final act, however, she recalls Lorenzo's “many vows of faith” and adds that they were “ne'er a true one”. The vows that justified her flight may themselves be deceptions, so the audience must weigh a daughter's escape from cruelty against the faithlessness of the romance that rewards it.

The final ring test is the play's last exercise in deception. Portia feigns anger that Bassanio has given away her ring, and Bassanio admits the loss rather than lie, saying that if he could “add a lie unto a fault” he would deny it. Portia replies that “void is your false heart of truth”. The accusation is part of her own staged trick, so the most accomplished deceiver in the play calls the honest man false. The reversal shows how readily deception is assigned to others, and it asks whether Portia's disguise belongs in the same category as the fault she imputes to Bassanio.

The play therefore invites a substantial reconsideration of deception, though not a complete one. It refuses to make deceit the trait of one religion or one outsider. Commerce, law, love and religion are each built on appearances, and the audience is asked to judge a deception by its motive and its cost rather than by its form. The comedy of the final act, in which the rings return and the lovers are reconciled, does not erase the cruelty of the trial. That unresolved tension is what makes the play's view of deception more complicated than its opening suggests.
sampleAnswers.feedback: This answer meets the 17-20 row: it evaluates how far the play invites reconsideration, sustains a thesis across the paragraphs and supports each claim with precise references to the bond, the caskets, the trial and the ring test. The strongest move is linking Shylock's taught villainy to the Christians' own deceptions. To lift it, the final paragraph could weigh more carefully where the play itself rewards deception, such as Portia's disguise or Jessica's flight.

sampleAnswers.answer:
The Merchant of Venice shows deception in several places, and the question asks whether this changes how the audience understands it. At the start Shylock makes a bond with Antonio and calls it a merry sport. If Antonio cannot repay the money, Shylock may take a pound of his flesh. Bassanio can see that the terms are fair in appearance but wicked. Antonio does not think the bond will be enforced because he expects his ships to come home, so he does not see the danger he is in. This shows that appearances can mislead, and it suggests that Shylock is not the only person who deceives.

At Belmont the caskets also test deception. The gold and silver caskets look more valuable than the lead, but they hold the wrong answers, and Bassanio chooses the plain lead. He says that the world is still deceived with ornament. This means that things which look good are not always good. The play then links this idea to law and religion, so that a person can seem good when he is not.

Portia disguises herself as Balthazar, a lawyer, and saves Antonio. She says the bond gives Shylock a pound of flesh but no jot of blood, so he cannot take any blood, and this trick works. Shylock loses his case. The Duke pardons his life, and Antonio asks that he become a Christian. Portia also makes a speech about mercy, which the audience may think is the moral point of the trial. Mercy is shown as better than justice, so the trial appears to end well.

Shylock argues that Jews have eyes and hands like Christians. He says that if Christians wrong Jews, they will take revenge, and that the villainy he has been taught he will carry out. This shows that deception can be learned. Jessica also deceives her father by running away with Lorenzo and taking his money. She feels ashamed of her disguise but still does it.

At the end, Portia tests Bassanio about the ring. She pretends to be angry that he gave it away. Bassanio tells her the truth, that he gave it to the lawyer. Portia then calls him false, even though she has been deceiving him. This shows that deception appears in many forms in the play, from the trial to the romance.

Overall, the play invites the audience to reconsider deception because many characters use false appearances. Some of their deceptions are presented as clever or necessary, and the reader must decide whether they are acceptable. The play's view of deception is therefore more complicated than the opening suggests.
sampleAnswers.feedback: This answer sits in the 9-12 row: it explains the play's deceptions in sequence and gives some relevant references, but it tends to retell the plot rather than argue about it. Its best point is that Portia accuses the honest Bassanio of falseness while deceiving him. To lift it, use precise quotations and make each paragraph test a single claim about whether a deception is justified.

sampleAnswers.answer: The Merchant of Venice has a lot of deception in it. Shylock makes a bond with Antonio, and if Antonio does not pay the money back Shylock can take a pound of his flesh. Antonio thinks the bond is kind but Bassanio is not sure about it. Antonio is worried about his ships and Shylock is angry about his money, so both of them have reasons to hide what they feel. Bassanio goes to Belmont to choose a casket to marry Portia and he picks the lead one because the others look better. Portia dresses up as a lawyer and wins the case for Antonio, and Shylock has to become a Christian. Jessica also runs away from her father and takes his money. Shylock is treated badly by the Christians but he is cruel too. At the end Portia tests Bassanio with a ring and everyone is happy. This shows that deception is a big part of the play, and people should think about whether it is right or wrong.
sampleAnswers.feedback: This answer sits in the 5-8 row: it retells the bond, the caskets and the trial in order, with no quotations and little sense of how the play handles deception. Its closing question about right and wrong is a real attempt at the topic. To lift it, choose one deception, quote the words that reveal it, and explain what the play asks the audience to think about it.

prompts.question: To what extent does the exploration of human experience in The Boy Behind the Curtain invite you to reconsider your understanding of independence?
markerNotes: The stem asks how far the book invites reconsideration, so the strongest answers take a position on the extent and qualify it, rather than listing what Winton is independent of.

The brake scene in Havoc: A Life in Accidents is the best evidence that a child's competence can be borrowed from a parent. Answers that see the father's teaching in it are stronger than those that read it only as bravery.
Twice on Sundays and The Wait and the Flow show independence as a choice made within a community. This lets strong answers avoid reading the book as a celebration of the lone individual.
Winton's adult revision of his verdict on Betsy is the book reconsidering its own judgements. An answer that finds this in the text has the reconsideration the question asks for.
commonStudentErrors: Treating independence only as being alone or self-sufficient, and never testing that idea against the church, family or surfing episodes.
Retelling the father's accident in Havoc: A Life in Accidents without asking what the brake scene shows about where Winton's competence comes from.
Presenting Winton's leaving of the church as simple heroism and ignoring the essay's ambivalence about the community he leaves.
Quoting remembered lines as exact wording instead of describing the scene and the technique precisely.
