Miller represents the emotions of The Crucible mainly through the features of drama rather than through description. Fear, guilt, jealousy, grief and pride are not reported to the audience; they are built through setting, stage action, dramatic irony, the pacing of dialogue and the climaxes of the courtroom and the jail. Written in 1953 as an allegory for McCarthyism, the play turns a collective panic into personal emotions, each tied to a particular character in a particular room. The human experiences it presents are therefore felt as well as understood.

The first act establishes the method. Parris's house is a place of fear and self-interest, where a minister frets over his position while his daughter lies motionless. Miller builds dramatic irony as Abigail deceives the adults around her. The audience learns that the dancing was an attempt to curse Elizabeth Proctor while Parris and the others are still deciding whom to believe, and that knowledge makes every accusation more frightening. Abigail's threats to the girls who might talk, that she can make them wish they had "never seen the sun go down", are delivered as raw menace, and the audience feels the danger before any official acts.

Act Two moves the play into the Proctor home, where fear becomes domestic. The poppet Mary Warren brings home is an ordinary object, but Cheever finds a needle inside it, and the object becomes evidence that carries fear from the court into the household. Miller lets the prop do emotional work: the audience watches a family home become a place where a poppet can lead to an arrest. The arrest follows so directly from the needle that the atmosphere of the court seems to have reached inside the Proctors' door.

Dialogue carries guilt in the same act. John Proctor's outburst moves from accusation to confession: "I'll plead no more!" is followed by the admission that his spirit twists around "the single error of my life". The line shows shame turning into anger, and its repeated exclamations make the self-reproach urgent. Elizabeth's grief has a similar force. Proctor describes an "everlasting funeral" that marches round her heart, and the image turns the marriage into a mourning that has no end.

The courtroom in Act Three is the emotional climax, and Miller stages it through noise, interruption and public exposure. Danforth's assertion that "No uncorrupted man may fear this court" makes fear itself a sign of guilt, and the audience recognises the irony in a court that treats fear as proof. When Proctor confesses his affair, private shame becomes public spectacle. The stage then fills with screaming girls, and Mary Warren, threatened with hanging, recants and joins them. Miller shows fear overcoming conscience through action the audience can watch, rather than through explanation.

The final act is set in the jail, and its emotional force comes from confinement. Proctor signs a confession, then tears it up. Miller's stage direction, "With the cry of his whole soul", tells the actor how to deliver the speech that follows, so the audience hears the emotion before it fully understands the argument. His line "Because it is my name" is a cry of pride, but it is also the moment at which guilt becomes a defence of identity. The confined space makes each line feel urgent, because there is nowhere left for Proctor to retreat.

Elizabeth expresses emotion more quietly, and Miller gives her a different register. She tells John that she counted herself "so plain" and that her suspicion made the house cold: "It were a cold house I kept". Her regret is staged through dialogue rather than action, and it changes how the audience reads her earlier coldness. Her answer to Hale, "He have his goodness now", is a refusal, and its force lies in its restraint. The contrast between the screaming court of Act Three and this quiet acceptance is one of the play's most deliberate effects.

Taken together, these features show that Miller does not treat emotion as a theme to be named. Fear is heard in the girls' screams, guilt is shown in a torn confession, and grief is embedded in a marriage that has gone cold. Staging, dialogue and dramatic irony work together so that the audience feels the cost of each emotion as the characters do. That is why the play's emotional power outlasts the particular accusations of its plot.

Shakespeare presents the emotions of The Merchant of Venice as things characters cannot fully explain, and the features of drama invite the audience to share that uncertainty. The play opens with Antonio saying, “I know not why I am so sad”, while his friends offer reasons that he rejects. Melancholy is represented as a state others try to diagnose and fail to understand. This sets up a pattern across the prescribed text: emotions arise from human experiences such as prejudice, humiliation, mercy and love, and each is revealed through staging, reported speech and song rather than direct statement.

Reported speech is one of drama's most effective tools for emotion. Solanio describes Shylock's cries in the street, quoting them as “My daughter! O my ducats! O my daughter!” The grief is real, but it reaches the audience through the account of a Venetian who treats it as a spectacle, so the emotion is both displayed and judged. Because we must reconstruct Shylock's loss from a hostile retelling, the scene turns his grief into a question about the listeners' cruelty rather than a simple expression of sorrow.

Asides allow the audience to hold feelings that characters conceal. When Shylock first sees Antonio, he remarks aside, “How like a fawning publican he looks!”, and vows to “feed fat the ancient grudge” he bears him. The men on stage cannot hear this hatred, but the audience does, so it understands Shylock's grievance before any bargain is struck. The public deal that follows is made in the shadow of that private speech, and its irony depends on the convention that the audience hears what the characters do not say aloud.

Shylock's humiliation is staged most fully in his defence of his humanity. He asks, “Hath not a Jew eyes?”, builds a list of the bodily and emotional features Jews share with Christians, and concludes that if Christians wrong him he will take revenge. The repeated questions give his rage a rhythm that mounts towards its close: “The villainy you teach me I will execute”. The emotion is not only anger but anger that the Christians have taught him, so his humiliation becomes a threat the audience can see is partly of their making.

The trial scene shows how quick exchanges and reversals produce emotional whiplash. Gratiano's repeated exclamations express a triumph the audience is invited to distrust. Portia's turn to “no jot of blood” removes Shylock's hope within a few lines, and his bitter reply, “the devil give him good of it”, turns despair into contempt. The emotional force comes from the speed of the exchange, with relief, elation and disbelief packed together. The audience knows Portia's identity and Shylock does not, so every appeal he makes is shaped by dramatic irony.

Portia's speech on mercy marks the play's highest emotional register. She begins, “The quality of mercy is not strain'd”, and describes it as falling “upon the place beneath”. The lyric imagery lifts compassion above the legal argument, yet it is addressed to a man who refuses it, and its pivot to law, “Therefore, Jew”, reminds us that the appeal to pity comes from a disguised woman. The emotion is persuasive and, in the light of the forced conversion that follows, uncomfortable.

Love is conveyed through music. A song is sung while Bassanio considers the caskets, asking, “Tell me where is fancy bred”, and answering that fancy is engendered in the eyes and “dies in the cradle where it lies”. The song gives his choice an emotional pressure the audience can feel, and it suggests that romantic feeling may be fragile. In the last act Lorenzo declares, “The man that hath no music in himself”, implying that music measures a person's feeling, and the moonlit exchanges that follow turn the lovers' passion into a shared, almost ritual register.

Jessica's shame is presented in private. After Launcelot leaves, she speaks alone and admits that she is “ashamed to be my father's child”. The soliloquy lets the audience hear her rejection of home directly rather than through the gossip of the Venetians, and the emotion is confessed before she acts on it.

Taken together, the features of drama make emotion in this play a matter of staging and perspective. Melancholy is left unexplained, grief is reported with mockery, hatred is confided in an aside, mercy is spoken in disguise, shame is confessed alone and love is set to music. The audience is not simply moved by these feelings. It is positioned to see how they are produced, displayed and judged, and that positioning is why the emotions of the prescribed text remain uneasy.

Shakespeare shows many emotions in The Merchant of Venice, and the features of drama help to show them. At the start Antonio is sad and his friends try to find out why. He says he does not know why he is sad, and they think it is because of his ships. This shows that Antonio's sadness is a feeling that cannot easily be explained. The audience has to wait to see what kind of sadness it is, and this is one of the first ways the play makes emotion a matter of mystery.

Shylock also has strong emotions. When Solanio tells how Shylock cried in the street about his daughter and his ducats, the audience hears about his grief. Solanio is making fun of him, which shows that the Venetians do not care about his feelings. This is an example of how emotions can be shown through what other characters say about them.

Shylock's emotions are also shown in the trial, where he is angry. He says that Jews have eyes and hands like Christians and that they should be able to get revenge when they are wronged. This shows his anger and humiliation. He says the villainy he has learnt from the Christians, which tells the audience that he is angry because of how he is treated. The court scene is also fast, and Gratiano keeps calling Portia a learned judge, which shows that the Christians are pleased with the result.

Portia's speech about mercy is very famous. It is a speech about how mercy is better than justice, and the audience can feel this emotion. Portia is disguised as a male lawyer, so the audience knows something that Shylock does not. This is called dramatic irony and it makes the trial more emotional.

Jessica is also emotional. She feels ashamed of her father and says that her house is hell. She speaks alone at the end of a scene and says she is ashamed to be his child. Her feelings are private at this point, which makes them different from the anger Shylock shows in public. This shows how she feels about her family.

The song sung while Bassanio chooses a casket is about love. It says that love begins in the eyes and can die. This suggests that love can be fragile. At the end of the play, the lovers talk under the moon and Lorenzo says that a man with no music in himself cannot be trusted.

Overall, Shakespeare uses drama to show emotions through different techniques. The audience sees the emotions of the characters and can understand how they feel, which makes the play interesting to watch.

sampleAnswers.answer:
Tim Winton represents emotion in The Boy Behind the Curtain as something to be examined, not merely felt. Through the features of nonfiction, especially the first-person retrospective voice, the linked essays and the citation of other texts, he lets a child’s fear, shame and wonder reach the page, and then has the adult narrator test what those feelings meant. The emotions arising from human experiences in the prescribed text are therefore shown in two registers at once: the immediacy of the moment and the judgement of a later life. The reader is moved, and is also invited to think.

Fear is the first emotion the collection renders with force. In Havoc: A Life in Accidents, Winton’s father, a police officer on a motorbike, is struck by a driver when Winton is about five, and the family’s stable life breaks apart. The dread is physical. The boy seeks out his father’s helmet. Later, at a roadside crash, the narrator recognises that his fear had echoed the dread of that first day. The retrospective voice does not simply report the feeling. It finds the pattern that links one fear to another, so the reader sees a childhood shaped by a single kind of dread.

The same dread returns in In the Shadow of the Hospital, where structure does much of the emotional work. The essay moves across decades, from a child who visits his father in hospital, to an adult who lives beside Fremantle Hospital for five years. The walk through the hospital to his father’s room is a “gauntlet of horrors”, and the hospital remained an image of horror. Feeling, in this essay, is stubborn. It outlasts reason, and the sequence of scenes lets the reader feel it accumulate over a lifetime.

Shame and humour are the subtler emotions, and they appear together in Betsy. The narrator’s grandfather drives an old Hillman Minx that the boy calls Betsy, and the boy is mortified to be seen in it. His friends laugh at their warped reflections in its rounded hubcaps, and the comedy is exact. But the comedy carries feeling, and the adult narrator does not let the child’s verdict stand. He admits that he judged the car too quickly, and he respects her durability, which is rare given what he calls “instant obsolescence”. A memoir allows the older self to revise what the younger one felt, and that revision is itself part of the emotional arc.

Joy and wonder receive a warmer treatment. In The Wait and the Flow, the thrill of riding a wave toward shore never gets old, and Winton keeps surfing until his skin hurts, accepting the pain for the happiness it brings. The essay presents delight as a choice made with full knowledge of its cost. Wonder is registered through the cultural references the book uses. At eight, Winton watches Kubrick’s 2001, which he describes as a “wormhole into the life of the imagination”, and the phrase shows how a film can turn a child’s attention toward a larger inner world.

The Demon Shark shows how feeling is shaped by what a person is shown. A childhood trailer for a documentary about a shark attack unsettles the boy, and by adulthood he has absorbed a public fear that owes more to media and politicians than to experience. The essay also draws on Peter Matthiessen’s account of a shark-filming expedition, and it includes his children’s question about why God made sharks. Its point is that bees kill more people each year yet provoke less fear. The emotion is represented as an inheritance, and the remedy it proposes is familiarity: people who spend time in the water tend to be less afraid of it.

Across these essays, the representation of emotion rests on three features: retrospection, which lets the adult correct the child; structure, which lets feeling accumulate across decades; and citation, which lets a private fear meet a wider record. The reader feels the father’s accident and the hospital corridors, and is also invited to ask whether the feelings were justified. In the prescribed text, then, emotion is a human experience that has been reflected on, not only lived through.
sampleAnswers.feedback: This answer meets the 17-20 row: it shows how retrospection, structure and citation shape emotions arising from human experiences, and it follows fear and shame across several essays as the adult narrator revises them. Its strongest move is the contrast between the child's verdict on Betsy and the adult's admission that he judged too quickly. The move that would lift it is to examine the diction or sentence rhythm of one passage, such as the opening of In the Shadow of the Hospital, rather than summarising its sequence.

Tim Winton shows emotions in The Boy Behind the Curtain through the way he tells his stories. Because he is writing about his own life, the feelings are his own, and he presents them as a memoir. The features of nonfiction, such as personal memory and a first-person voice, make the reader feel close to him and to the people in his life. The emotions arising from human experiences are personal and easy to recognise.

In the essay Havoc: A Life in Accidents, Winton describes his father being hurt in a motorbike accident. The narrator was scared, and this fear is important in the essay. Later, when the narrator is older, he recognises that he was frightened again at a roadside crash. This shows that fear can come back over time. The helmet his father wore makes the fear concrete.

The essay In the Shadow of the Hospital shows Winton afraid of hospitals again. He remembers visiting his father in hospital when he was a child. The walk through the hospital is frightening, and he calls it a “gauntlet of horrors”. As an adult he still feels uncomfortable in hospitals, even though he knows they are places of care. This shows that emotions can last a long time.

Winton also writes about shame in Betsy. He is embarrassed about his grandfather’s car, and his friends laugh at it. Later he thinks that he judged it too quickly. This is a good example of how memoir allows the author to look back and change his view of what he felt.

Joy appears in The Wait and the Flow, where Winton describes surfing and how happy it makes him. He says the thrill of catching a wave is worth the pain of his skin hurting. This shows the emotions are not always negative.

The Demon Shark shows that Winton thinks people fear sharks for the wrong reasons. He notes that bees kill more people each year but provoke less fear. He also says people who spend time in the water are less afraid. These points use evidence to argue against fear.

The features of nonfiction help Winton represent emotions in the book. The first-person voice makes the feelings personal, and the essays about different times in his life show how emotions change. Through these features the reader understands the human experiences in the book, and the prescribed text becomes a record of feeling.

Its strength is the observation that the memoir lets the adult revise the child's fear. The move that would lift it is to choose one passage and trace a specific technique, such as the concrete detail of the helmet, through to its emotional effect.

In another essay he is embarrassed about a car called Betsy because his friends make fun of it. He likes surfing and feels happy when he catches a wave, even though it hurts his skin. He also writes about sharks and says people are scared of them. These emotions are part of the human experiences in the book. Winton uses his own life to show these feelings, which is what nonfiction does, so the features of nonfiction help show the emotions.

Yousafzai and Lamb represent the emotions arising from human experiences mainly through the features of nonfiction that a memoir makes possible: a first-person voice, a retrospective view, a chronological shape and a documentary sense of place. The emotions are not announced in the abstract. They are built through particular experiences, from fear on the road to school to grief at the closure of girls' schools, and the reader feels them because the prescribed text places them inside one life. Christina Lamb's background as a journalist also sets Malala's experience within the wider history of Swat, which connects emotion to context rather than leaving it as private feeling.

First-person narration is the most important feature. Because the story is told by Malala, the fear of Taliban rule is felt from the inside. She writes about threats and violence as experienced by a girl who wants to go to school, and the reader is positioned to share her anxiety. The retrospective perspective adds a second emotional layer. The adult narrator looks back on her younger self with a mixture of pride and distance, so the frightened girl is presented with tenderness rather than with pity alone. The memoir thus represents fear as something lived through and understood, not simply reported.

The early sections on Swat use the documentary qualities of nonfiction to build emotion. The ban on girls' schooling, which took effect in Mingora in January 2009, is delivered as historical fact, but it carries the grief of a student watching her school and her classmates' futures close down. Her blog, written under the name Gul Makai for the BBC, gives the reader the immediacy of a diary, and the memoir shows the anxiety of writing while afraid. The mixture of public fact and private feeling allows the book to represent fear and resolve together, which is one of its central emotional arguments.

The attack on 9 October 2012 is the emotional centre of the memoir. The narration moves to a short, vivid account of the bus, the gunman and the shooting, and the prose becomes more immediate. Emotion here is represented through shock and disorientation as much as through reflection. A survivor can report what happened and also admit gaps in what she remembers, and this honesty doubles the emotional effect, since the reader feels both the violence of the event and the uncertainty of its aftermath. Nonfiction gives the account a credibility that makes this scene land with unusual force.

The later sections turn to grief, dependence and recovery. The account of waking in Birmingham, learning to walk again and facing an operation to repair her face gives emotion a bodily dimension. The memoir's description of her parents' distress shows love and fear in their most personal form. The inclusion of the family's own experience, including her mother's difficulty adjusting to life in England, widens the emotional range beyond Malala herself. The features of nonfiction allow the reader to feel the cost of the attack for everyone around her.

Hope is also represented, though not sentimentally. Malala's commitment to education is shown as an emotion as well as a cause: her love of learning, her attachment to her father's school and her wish to return to her studies. The closing sections move outward to education for all children, and the hope feels earned because the reader has already shared the fear and the recovery that precede it.

Christina Lamb's role also shapes how emotion is represented. Her journalistic habit of setting out facts, dates and places tempers the intensity of the personal narrative, so that emotion does not become melodrama. The reader sees the Taliban's rule as a political system and as a set of human experiences, with fear as a response to real events. This restraint is not coldness. It allows anger, sorrow and admiration to register with more force because the authors do not ask for them directly.

Overall, Yousafzai and Lamb represent emotion through features of nonfiction that bind feeling to experience: first-person narration, retrospective reflection, documentary context, and an honest account of injury and recovery. Fear, grief, love and hope are not explained to the reader but felt through particular scenes. The prescribed text is most powerful where it lets the reader watch a frightened girl become a determined one, without pretending that the change was easy.
sampleAnswers.feedback: This answer meets the 17-20 row: it analyses how first-person narration, retrospection and documentary context produce fear, grief and hope, tying each feature to a particular scene. The strongest move is the account of the bus attack and the uncertainty of memory it admits. To lift it further, support the point about documentary context with a closely worded passage from the memoir.

Yousafzai and Lamb represent emotion through the features of nonfiction. The memoir is written in the first person, so the reader sees events through Malala's eyes. This is why the fear of living under the Taliban comes across so strongly. The book describes the ban on girls' schools, and the reader can feel how frustrating and sad this is.

Another feature is the retrospective voice. Malala looks back on her younger self, which lets her show how she felt at the time and how she understands those feelings now. She is not afraid all the time, and this makes her seem more real to the reader. The reader can also see the love of her family, particularly her father, who supports her education and her right to go to school.

The attack on the bus is the most emotional part of the book. The reader learns about the gunman and the shooting, and the shock is clear. The memoir then moves to the hospital in Birmingham, where Malala has to learn to walk again. This shows the physical side of her suffering and her determination to recover, and it makes the reader sympathise with her.

The family's feelings also matter. Her parents are worried about her, and her mother finds life in a new country hard. These experiences show that the attack affected everyone around her, not only Malala. The emotions are therefore spread across the whole family.

The authors also use the prescribed text to show hope. Malala wants to return to school and is committed to education for all children. This hope shows her character and ends the memoir on a positive note. Overall, the authors represent emotions well through these features, and the reader is able to share Malala's fear, sadness and hope.

In the prescribed text, Stephen Daldry represents the emotions arising from human experiences through the features of film, and rarely through what characters say. Billy Elliot seldom tells the audience what a character feels. Instead, emotion is attached to a space, an object, a sound or a silence, and each of these carries a cost. Shock, anger, grief and joy each have a feature that makes them visible and makes them weigh on the people in the story.

The gym is the film's central space. Billy's father sends him there to learn boxing, but the ballet class meets in the gym because the usual basement studio has become a soup kitchen for the striking miners. The mise-en-scene therefore places two ideas of discipline in one room: the boxing that stands for the family's expectations of masculinity, and the ballet that stands for Billy's own wish. When Jackie catches Billy and Michael dancing there, the shock is built into the setting, because the room where his father sent him to box has become the place where the son's passion is revealed. Jackie is stunned, and the emotion is carried by the discovery rather than by any speech.

Grief is carried by an object rather than a speech. Billy's mother has died, and the family has so little money that Jackie pawns her jewellery to pay for the London trip. The film does not need a eulogy. A small transaction, giving up something that belonged to the dead woman, carries a widowed father's grief and his love for his son in one gesture. The feature here is narrative rather than visual: what is sold, and what it meant, make the audience feel the loss without being told. Daldry himself named grief among the film's themes, and the pawned jewellery is where that theme becomes concrete.

Anger is shaped by the strike and by the film's sound. Tony's arrest in a clash between police and striking miners costs Billy his first audition, so the public anger of the picket line reaches into the family's most private hope. The soundtrack gives the restlessness of the town a rhythm. Its glam rock and punk songs, including the T. Rex tracks on the album, drive the film's energy, and sound becomes as much a carrier of feeling as the events it accompanies. Anger here is not only shown in violence but heard in the music.

Joy is represented most precisely in the London audition, where Billy's feeling resists language. Earlier in the audition he punches another boy in frustration and fears he has ruined his chances. When the panel asks what dancing feels like, he struggles for words and says it is "like electricity". The hesitation before the answer, and the inadequacy of the phrase, represent emotion as something that exceeds speech. The panel asks for an explanation and the film withholds a clear one, so the audience understands his joy through his failure to describe it.

The closing flash-forward represents pride as a delayed and public emotion. In 1998, the adult Billy dances as the Swan in Matthew Bourne's Swan Lake, with Jackie, Tony and Michael watching from the audience, and Jackie is overcome with astonishment and pride. Tchaikovsky's score gives the scene the weight of an occasion the family has earned. What matters most is who is watching. Jackie, whose pride has been tested throughout, sees the result of what he gave up, so the emotion is attached to the people who paid for it.

To a large extent, then, Daldry represents emotion through the features of film. The film's strength is that feeling is not announced but made to cost something: a shared gym, a pawned object, a silence in an audition and a father in an audience. The method depends on the audience recognising these spaces and objects as carriers of feeling, and a viewer without some sense of the 1984 strike may miss what the pawned jewellery and the picket line cost the family. Daldry's achievement is that the costs are visible, and the emotion arises from what the characters give up.
sampleAnswers.feedback: This answer meets the 17-20 row: it analyses how the gym, the pawned jewellery, the audition silence and the closing performance carry specific emotions, and it ties each feature to a named scene. Its strength is the reading of the pawned jewellery as grief carried by an object rather than by dialogue. The move that would lift it is to add one more precise feature of film, such as a shot or an edit, to the closing sequence.

Daldry uses the features of film to show emotions in Billy Elliot. The most important setting is the gym. Billy's dad sends him there to learn boxing, but the ballet class has to use the gym while the usual basement studio is a soup kitchen for the striking miners. This shows how the strike has changed the town. When Jackie finds Billy dancing in the gym with Michael, he is stunned, and the audience can see his shock. This emotion comes from the experience of a father who did not expect his son to be different.

Grief is another emotion. Billy's mother has died, and the family has very little money. Jackie pawns Billy's mother's jewellery to pay for the trip to London. This shows that Jackie loves his son and misses his wife. The jewellery belonged to his wife, so giving it up shows how much he is prepared to lose. The jewellery is an object that the film uses to show the family's sacrifice, so the audience understands the cost without being told.

Anger is shown through the strike. Tony is arrested in a clash between police and striking miners, and Billy misses his audition. The audience feels angry about this because it seems unfair. The audience knows what the strike costs the family, so the anger feels personal rather than political. The songs on the soundtrack are energetic and help show the rebellious feeling of the town.

At the audition, Billy is nervous and punches another boy. When the panel asks him what dancing feels like, he has trouble answering and says it is like electricity. This shows that joy is hard to put into words, and the film shows this through his silence. The panel's question makes his feeling a public matter.

At the end, the adult Billy performs in Matthew Bourne's Swan Lake and his father is proud. The music is by Tchaikovsky, which makes the scene emotional. The ending gives the audience Jackie's reaction, which is where the emotion of the film settles. Overall, the film creates emotion through the setting, the objects, the music and the dialogue, so the audience feels these emotions strongly.

Ivan O’Mahoney represents emotion in Go Back to Where You Came From mostly through the features of media rather than through the participants' words alone. The prescribed text, made up of Series 1 Episodes 1 to 3 and The Response, combines narration, editing, interviews, original music and a studio follow-up, and each feature steers the viewer towards a particular feeling. The emotions the series produces are fear, unease, sympathy and a sense of accumulating distress. The series makes them arise from its structure as much as from the human experiences it films.

The narration is the first feature to consider. The voice-over, delivered by the actor Colin Friels, supplies political and geographic background, and its calm, informative register works against the emotions it accompanies. When the boat crossing ends in a rescue at sea, the narration places the experience in a wider context, so the viewer is invited to see the distress as typical rather than exceptional. The effect is to turn fear into understanding, which keeps the emotion from becoming purely personal. The viewer is asked to feel and to reason at once, and that double demand is central to the series' emotional method.

Editing shapes the emotional starting point. In the first episode, tightly constructed backstory packages introduce each participant with background and a stated view. These packages establish the position the series will test, so any later discomfort is measured against it. The emotion is not simply presented; it is set up, and this set-up is what makes the later shift feel earned. Editing also intercuts direct experience with expert opinion. A participant's raw reaction is followed by an explanation of the conditions behind it, and the cut between the two sharpens each emotion because neither stands alone.

Interviews carry the emotion into conversation. Participants question the former refugees who host them about why they live in Australia and how they arrived. Sympathy is most likely to arise here, because the hosts are no longer types or statistics but individuals describing their own lives. The participants' questions can also produce discomfort for the viewer, since the answers expose the gap between the views the participants brought and the histories they now hear. The interview is the feature that most directly connects the viewer's emotion to a particular person.

The original music and the documentary footage, which is often confronting, work together on the emotional register. The footage makes the camps and the slums feel immediate, while the music supports that register rather than working against it. The combination matters most in the later stages of the journey. The emotional arc moves from the sudden fear of a boat rescue to the grinding conditions of a camp in Kenya, then to the slums of Jordan and the open violence of Goma and Baghdad. Because the route is taken in reverse, the emotions build cumulatively, and O’Mahoney presents distress as the result of accumulated experience rather than as a single shock.

The Response adds a further layer. Held before a studio audience of families, friends, refugees and advocates, it returns to a highlights package of the most extreme moments, and the participants respond both to that footage and to the public reaction. The viewer watches the distress replayed and watches the participants react to their own images. This doubles the emotional experience, which was felt once in the field and is felt again in the studio. It also raises a question about manipulation, since the most intense moments are selected again for an audience that already holds a position.

Overall, O’Mahoney represents emotion skilfully because the features of the form make feelings arise from structure. The narration makes distress understood, the editing sets a starting position and then tests it, the interviews make sympathy personal, the music and footage give weight to the images, and the studio follow-up carries the response to a wider public. The limit is that the most intense emotion belongs to the people the participants meet, and the viewer encounters it through a carefully built frame. The series is most convincing when it lets the viewer see that frame as a choice, and that is the point at which its emotions become a matter of judgement rather than simple reaction.
sampleAnswers.feedback: This answer meets the 17-20 row: it analyses how emotion is produced through several features of the form and ties each feature to a specific effect on the viewer, from the narration to the studio replay. The references to the first episode's backstory packages and the hosts' interviews are well chosen. To lift it further, the final paragraph could test the claim that the emotions are shaped more directly by selection, rather than only raising the question.

In Waste Land, Lucy Walker represents the emotions of the catadores mainly through the features of media that shape how the audience experiences their lives: the setting, the staging of the portraits, the editing that moves between the landfill and the warehouse, and the score by Moby. The emotions arising from human experiences in the film are not simple. Dignity and despair sit side by side in the same people, and the film's media choices keep both in view. The audience feels unease at the dump, but the film's larger movement is towards pride, self-recognition and a guarded hope.

The film establishes its audience inside the world of the landfill. Jardim Gramacho was one of the largest landfills in the world, and the pickers spend their days in its refuse without the security of conventional employment. Walker does not hide the despair this produces. Her media choices do this work through the setting itself, through close attention to individual faces, and through the chance for the pickers to describe their own lives. Isis's breakdown, in which she reveals the tragedy that brought her to the dump, is the most direct expression of grief in the film. It turns a statistic about waste into a loss the audience can feel.

Walker's most powerful structural choice is to follow the process of making the portraits. The film moves from the photograph taken at the landfill to the projection on the floor of a warehouse, then to the slow work of gathering materials and reassembling the image, and finally to the completed photograph. This sequence builds emotion through anticipation. The audience watches the pickers gather the materials of their daily labour and turn them into likenesses of themselves, so that the rubbish they handle every day becomes the medium through which they are seen. The emotional payoff is recognition, and the film allows that feeling to arrive gradually rather than announcing it.

The score by Moby carries much of the emotional shift. Its job is to support the cutting between the landfill and the warehouse, so that the two spaces sit within one emotional register. The music does not replace the pickers' own feelings. It lets the audience share their growing involvement without the film having to name it. This is where the features of media work together: the editing decides what we see next, and the score shapes how we feel about it.

The film also represents warmth and joy, which matter as much as grief. The pickers display remarkably good spirits and camaraderie, and the friendships that form among them give the film a human texture beyond hardship. Valter, the group's elder statesman and recycling guru, delights in rhymes and morals, so the audience meets a man whose emotions are generous and playful rather than defeated. The film gives these moments room, which makes them more affecting than summary would.

The strongest emotional turn is towards pride. The pickers report that the project has lifted some of the stigma attached to their work, and the film's emotional arc arrives at this change: people used to being overlooked now have their images displayed as art. The final photograph is large-scale and presents each picker as a figure of dignity rather than someone associated with refuse. The pride is real, but it is hard-won, and the film never lets the audience forget the work and the cost behind it.

The hope has a sober edge. The landfill closed in June 2012, and the community built on the dump belonged to a world that was ending. Walker's media choices hold hope and loss together: the final images are beautiful, but the audience knows the work is precarious. Despair is not replaced by hope. It sits beside it, so the emotions the film creates are complex rather than simple uplift.

Walker therefore represents emotion through the whole structure of the documentary rather than through any single statement. Grief, humour, pride and hope are all present, and they reach the audience through editing, sound and the staging of the portraits. The features of media do the work that the catadores' own words only begin, and that is why the emotions the film creates feel earned.
sampleAnswers.feedback: This answer meets the 17-20 row: it shows how several features of media combine to create grief, pride and hope, and it keeps despair and dignity in tension rather than resolving them. Its strength is the close reading of the portrait process as an emotional structure. To lift it, the final paragraph could say more about the moment of recognition and how the framing of the final photograph makes the audience feel it.

sampleAnswers.answer:
Waste Land shows emotion through the features of media, and in this film the emotions come from people working at a landfill near Rio de Janeiro. Lucy Walker directs the documentary and uses setting, editing, music and the portraits to show how the catadores feel about their lives. This answer explains some of the features that create emotion in the film.

The first feature is the setting. The landfill is shown as a dangerous and unpleasant place, and this creates a sense of sadness and unease that the audience shares. Walker keeps the camera close enough that the place feels uncomfortable to be in. The pickers work in the rubbish every day, and the film shows that the work is hard. Their situation creates feelings of despair, which the audience can see in the faces of the people. Isis is one example, because she breaks down when she talks about what brought her to the dump.

The second feature is the process of making the portraits. Muniz photographs the catadores, projects the photographs on the warehouse floor and asks the pickers to make the pictures from rubbish. This creates a feeling of pride because the pickers are able to make something beautiful. The audience feels happy when the final photographs appear, because they show the workers in a positive way.

The third feature is the music. Moby wrote the score, and the music makes the film more emotional. When the pickers become more involved in the work, the music helps the audience feel more hopeful.

Walker also shows the friendships among the pickers, and this makes them seem like people rather than workers. Valter tells rhymes and morals, which shows his humour and warmth. These moments help the audience feel close to the catadores.

The money also helps the pickers. Muniz gives the proceeds to the association, and the money is used for trucks, schooling and a library. This makes the pickers feel proud and gives them hope for the future. The pickers report that the project has lifted some of the stigma attached to picking rubbish, which is another emotional result. The film does not present these changes as complete, and the audience sees some of the difficulty the pickers still face.
sampleAnswers.feedback: This answer sits in the 9-12 row: it names several features and the emotion each produces, but the explanation stays at the level of effect and the references are thin and general. Its clear strength is the link between the portrait process and pride. To lift it, analyse one feature in detail, such as how the move from the landfill to the warehouse changes the audience's feeling, and support it with a specific moment.

sampleAnswers.answer: Waste Land is a documentary by Lucy Walker about Vik Muniz, an artist who makes pictures out of rubbish. The pickers at the dump are shown to be sad and happy at different times. The film has music by Moby and it shows the photographs being made. The pickers make pictures of themselves and this makes them feel good about what they do. The emotions in the film are sad when the pickers talk about their lives and happy when the pictures are finished. The film uses editing to show these things, and it moves between the dump and the warehouse. The audience sees the pickers working together, and this gives a different feeling to the scenes at the dump. So the film represents emotions in a good way, and people will probably enjoy watching it because it is interesting and shows a lot of feelings.
sampleAnswers.feedback: This answer sits in the 5-8 row: it describes the film and names emotions in general terms, but it does not show how any feature of media produces a particular feeling. Its strength is the correct identification of the portraits as the emotional centre of the film. To lift it, choose one feature, such as the music or the cut from the dump to the warehouse, and say what the audience feels at that moment.

prompts.scenario: Your answer will be assessed on how well you: demonstrate understanding of human experiences in texts; analyse, explain and assess the ways human experiences are represented in texts; organise, develop and express ideas using language appropriate to audience, purpose and context.
prompts.hscSection: Paper 1, Section II — Texts and Human Experiences (20 marks). Allow about 45 minutes.

prompts.question: ‘A text can ignite ideas about collective human experiences that enrich our view of the world.’ To what extent do you agree with this statement in relation to your prescribed text? In your response, make close reference to your prescribed text.
markerNotes: The statement asks for a judgement about extent, so the strongest answers state a clear position on the statement and qualify it by reference to the text.
Collective experience is shown through specific people and events. Answers should show how a shared experience is carried by these details, rather than generalising about a country or group.
The statement links collective experience to how we see the world. The strongest answers explain what the text changes in that view, and where its ideas are limited or contested.
Close reference matters most here: one detail from the text, quoted briefly and explained, outweighs a summary of its plot or chapters.
commonStudentErrors: Summarising the central events of the text without assessing the statement.
Treating one character's story as representative of a whole group, without noticing the narrator's or the text's particular position.
Overstating the text's effect on the world, for example by claiming it solved a problem it depicts.
Writing about a character's courage as a personal virtue alone, without linking it to the shared experiences of the community the text depicts.
keywords: enrich our view of the world
prompts.markingCriteria:
17-20 marks: Evaluates skilfully the extent to which the prescribed text ignites ideas about collective human experiences that enrich our view of the world; Presents an insightful response supported by well-chosen textual references from the prescribed text; Writes a coherent and sustained response using language appropriate for audience, purpose and context
13-16 marks: Evaluates effectively the extent to which the prescribed text ignites ideas about collective human experiences that enrich our view of the world; Presents a thoughtful response supported by relevant textual references from the prescribed text; Writes an organised response using language appropriate for audience, purpose and context
9-12 marks: Explains the extent to which the prescribed text ignites ideas about collective human experiences that enrich our view of the world; Presents a response supported by some textual references from the prescribed text; Writes a response using variable control of language appropriate for audience and purpose
5-8 marks: Expresses limited understanding of the extent to which the prescribed text ignites ideas about collective human experiences that enrich our view of the world; Describes aspects of the prescribed text; Writes a response with minimal control of language
1-4 marks: Refers to the prescribed text in a minimal way; Attempts to compose a response

sampleAnswers.answer:
I am Malala tells two stories at once. One is the personal story of a girl who wanted to go to school. The other is the collective story of the people of the Swat Valley, where the Taliban closed girls' schools and turned education into a public contest. To what extent the statement holds depends on how far the memoir's shared experiences reach beyond its narrator. I argue that Malala Yousafzai's book does ignite ideas about collective human experiences that enrich our view of the world, though its vision is shaped by one family's position and by the controversy it provoked.

The shared experience begins in the family's commitment to education. Her father, Ziauddin, opened the Khushal School, and her mother, Toor Pekai, brought children in need into the household, while Ziauddin gave free places in his schools to poor children. Schooling in this memoir is a family and community enterprise rather than a private privilege. The collective threat arrives through the Taliban's “Radio Mullah” broadcasts, which condemned music and dancing and told women to stay at home. The restriction reaches every household in the valley, so the family's private loss becomes a community's loss.

The shooting on 9 October 2012 gives the collective its clearest image. After an exam, two men stopped her school bus, and one asked who Malala was before firing. Her friends Shazia and Kainat were also injured, so the attack falls on a group of students rather than on one girl alone. The memoir names one of its sections “Three Bullets, Three Girls”, which frames the attack as a shared event as well as a personal wound. The book makes the reader see the injured body as the place where a public struggle over education is fought.

The collective extends far beyond Swat. Malala received many cards after the attack, and she spent months in hospital in Birmingham, where she worried about where her father was and about the cost of treatment, which the Pakistani government covered. Her recovery depended on governments, doctors and strangers who sent messages across borders. A personal wound becomes a public story, and the memoir shows that a girl's survival is measured in shared attention as well as in surgery. The question of girls' schooling becomes a matter of international concern.

The book's reception shows that its ideas ignite argument as well as sympathy. The All Pakistan Private School's Federation announced that the book would be banned in its 152,000 member institutions, saying that it disrespected Islam, and the Pakistani Taliban threatened bookshops that sold it. These responses are part of the collective experience the memoir reveals: a world in which a girl's account of schooling can be read as either an attack on faith or a demand for justice. The book enriches our view of the world not by settling the question, but by making the contest visible.

The qualification is that the memoir's collective is shaped by one family's position. Her father owned schools, which gave the family a standing that many families in the valley did not have. The book was co-written with Christina Lamb, and one reviewer objected to the voice of a foreign correspondent running alongside Malala's. The memoir ignites ideas about shared suffering, but it speaks most clearly for a girl with a platform, so readers must look elsewhere for the voices of girls who had none.

Yet the statement largely holds. The memoir's most enduring idea is that education is a right that no single family can secure alone, and that idea depends on the collective. Malala's own ambition, to be known for fighting for education, moves the story from self to shared cause. The book ignites ideas about collective human experiences, and in doing so it asks readers to see Swat not as a remote place but as part of a wider world in which girls are denied a classroom.
sampleAnswers.feedback: This answer meets the 17-20 row: it takes a clear position on the extent of the statement, qualifies it through the memoir's narrator and its reception, and anchors each claim in specific events such as the bus shooting and the Khushal School. The move that would lift it further is to sharpen the final paragraph by naming one image from the memoir that carries the collective idea, rather than relying on the general claim that education is a right.

sampleAnswers.answer:
I am Malala is a memoir about a girl who wanted an education and was shot by the Taliban. It describes her life in the Swat Valley and her father's schools. Her father, Ziauddin, opened a school called the Khushal School, and he gave free places to poor children. Her mother also brought children who needed help into their home. This shows that education was a shared activity in the family and the community, and it helps explain why the Taliban's actions affected so many people.

The Taliban grew powerful in Swat and banned girls from school. Malala describes the radio broadcasts that criticised music and dancing and told women to stay at home. She also wrote a blog for the BBC in Urdu under a pseudonym, which shows how she was already speaking out before she was shot. Her school was shut down after a Taliban order in 2009, and her family had to move away for a few months. These events show a collective situation, because many families had to make the same kinds of decisions.

On 9 October 2012, two men stopped the school bus that Malala was travelling on and shot her and two of her friends. Malala survived and was flown to hospital in Birmingham. The shooting is the most dramatic event in the book, and it shows how far the Taliban were prepared to go. Malala's friends were also hurt, which makes the attack about more than one girl. Malala received thousands of cards from people around the world, which shows that her story reached beyond Pakistan.

The memoir has also caused debate. Some private schools in Pakistan banned it, saying it disrespected Islam, and the Pakistani Taliban threatened bookshops that sold it. This suggests that the book has ideas that people find controversial. Overall the book tells a story about education and courage, and it helps readers understand the experience of girls in Swat, although it is written from Malala's point of view and so does not show every person's experience.
sampleAnswers.feedback: This answer sits in the 9-12 row: it explains the Swat background and the shooting in order and identifies the collective effects, but it mostly describes the events and rarely analyses how the memoir presents them. Its strength is the accurate account of the school closure and the family's displacement. The move that would lift it is to take one passage, such as the bus attack and the friends who were hurt, and explain how the telling makes the attack a shared experience.

sampleAnswers.answer: I am Malala is about a girl from Pakistan who was shot by the Taliban because she wanted to go to school. She grew up in the Swat Valley, and her father ran schools there. The Taliban closed the girls' schools, and her family had to leave for a time. In 2012 she was shot on her school bus. She was flown to hospital in England and survived. The book also explains that many people supported her, and that the book itself has been banned in some places. The story shows that education is important and that girls should have the right to go to school.
sampleAnswers.feedback: This answer sits in the 5-8 row: it describes Malala's shooting and move to Birmingham without analysing how the memoir represents collective experience. It offers no textual reference beyond the main events. The move that would lift it is to name one passage or event from the book and explain how it presents the experience of many girls, not only Malala.

prompts.scenario: Your answer will be assessed on how well you: demonstrate understanding of human experiences in texts; analyse, explain and assess the ways human experiences are represented in texts; organise, develop and express ideas using language appropriate to audience, purpose and context.
prompts.hscSection: Paper 1, Section II — Texts and Human Experiences (20 marks). Allow about 45 minutes.

prompts.question: In what ways has the study of your prescribed text given you insights into the complex relationship between human qualities, motivations and actions? In your response, make close reference to your prescribed text.
markerNotes: The question asks in what ways the study of the text has given insight, so the strongest responses offer several connected ways, each developed through the text, rather than one point repeated across the response.

Motivation is the hinge of the question. Strong answers show how a quality shapes what a person wants, and how that want drives an action that tests or reveals the quality. A response that lists a quality, a motive and an action in sequence has not yet shown a relationship.

The word complex asks for tension. The best responses show that a quality can be admirable and harmful at once, or that one motive produces contradictory actions, and they test that tension against the text rather than resolving it neatly.
Close reference carries the argument. A few well-chosen quotations or moments, each analysed for what it shows about the relationship, are worth more than general references to the text as a whole.
commonStudentErrors: Retelling the plot of the text, or summarising what happens, rather than explaining how studying it has given insight into the relationship.
Treating human qualities, motivations and actions as three separate lists, so the response never explains how one leads to another.
Making broad claims about human nature with no close reference to a particular moment, image or line in the prescribed text.
Quoting the text without analysing how the quotation shows a quality, a motive or an action at work.
prompts.markingCriteria:
17-20 marks: Explains skilfully the ways in which the study of their prescribed text gives them insights into the complex relationship between human qualities, motivations and actions; Presents a perceptive response supported by well-chosen textual references from the prescribed text; Writes a coherent and sustained response using language appropriate to audience, purpose and context
13-16 marks: Explains effectively the ways in which the study of their prescribed text gives them insights into the complex relationship between human qualities, motivations and actions; Presents a thoughtful response supported by relevant textual references from the prescribed text; Writes an organised response using language appropriate to audience, purpose and context
9-12 marks: Explains the ways in which the study of their prescribed text gives them insights into the complex relationship between human qualities, motivations and actions; Presents a response supported by some textual references from the prescribed text; Writes a response using variable control of language appropriate to audience, purpose and context
5-8 marks: Expresses limited understanding of the ways in which the study of their prescribed text gives them insights into the complex relationship between human qualities, motivations and actions; Describes aspects of the prescribed text; Writes a response with limited control of language
1-4 marks: Refers to the prescribed text in a minimal way; Attempts to compose a response

sampleAnswers.answer:
The study of my prescribed text has shown me that human qualities, motivations and actions form a loop rather than a chain. A quality is not simply the cause of an action. Motivations decide which qualities come to the surface, and each action then changes the qualities people believe they possess. In Shakespeare’s The Merchant of Venice, the bargain between Antonio and Shylock, the courtship of Portia and the trial that closes the play make this loop visible. In the text, qualities are revealed, distorted or hardened by what a person wants and by the community around them.

Prejudice is the quality the play places at the centre of its conflict, and its most important effect is to generate motivation. Antonio calls Shylock a “cut-throat dog” and has spat upon his “Jewish gaberdine”. These insults become the foundation of Shylock’s revenge. When he asks “Hath not a Jew eyes?”, he argues for a shared human feeling, and then he turns that argument into a justification: “If you wrong us, shall we not revenge?” The speech makes his motive intelligible. Yet the action he chooses, the insistence on a pound of flesh, shows how revenge hardens into cruelty. A prejudice produces a motive, and that motive produces an action that seems to confirm the prejudice.

Money is the motive that most often disguises the other qualities. Bassanio needs three thousand ducats to pursue Portia, and the loan he secures on Antonio’s guarantee ties love to money from the start. Portia’s suitors make the link explicit, since each chooses a casket that promises what he desires. The Prince of Morocco chooses gold, opens it and finds a skull and a verse beginning “All that glisters is not gold”. Bassanio approaches the choice differently. He reflects that “The world is still deceived with ornament”, and he chooses plain lead. His humility wins Portia, but it is also a motive, since he has chosen to be seen as honest. The quality that wins is real, yet it is inseparable from the wish to be loved.

Loyalty gives Antonio’s actions their weight. He accepts the bond because he wants Bassanio to succeed, and the risk he takes is out of all proportion to the money. His melancholy at the opening, “I know not why I am so sad”, suggests a man already exposed by his attachments. At the trial he calls himself “a tainted wether of the flock”, ready for death. Loyalty is admirable, but here it leaves him resigned to a fate he did not choose. Devotion to a friend makes him reckless, and that recklessness makes him vulnerable to the hatred of his enemy.

Belonging links love, identity and action most clearly. Jessica flees her father’s house, driven by a wish to escape a home she finds oppressive and to join a community that will accept her. Her self-judgement is harsh. She wonders what heinous sin it is “To be ashamed to be my father’s child”, and she distances herself from him: “I am not to his manners.” Her honesty about her own discomfort is a quality, yet her escape is deceptive: she takes his ducats and jewels. Shylock’s cry, as Solanio mockingly reports it, “My daughter! O my ducats! O my daughter!”, fuses love with property, so his sense of belonging to her is bound up with what she carries away. Her elopement reveals the complex relationship between love, money and identity. The motives that free her are the same ones that make her the source of her father’s grief.

The trial makes the play’s clearest claim about qualities and motives. Portia asks Shylock to show mercy in a speech that begins, “The quality of mercy is not strained”, and she argues that mercy is “enthroned in the hearts of kings”. Yet the speech is addressed to a man driven by revenge, and it fails because Shylock does not feel the quality it asks for. Portia’s own mercy is conditional. She grants the bond, then declares that it gives Shylock “no jot of blood”. His motive is turned against him, and the penalty is forced conversion and the loss of his property. The mercy the Christians display therefore depends on power. Mercy and justice, which the speech sets against each other, become instruments of a stronger motive: the wish to defeat an enemy and protect a friend.

Qualities, motives and actions are bound together in ways that resist easy judgement. Prejudice produces revenge, revenge produces cruelty, and cruelty is answered by a display of mercy that is shaped by power. Love and money run through one another, so that a courtship needs a loan and a daughter’s escape is measured in ducats. Loyalty can be a person’s finest quality and also the reason he is willing to die. Each quality takes its meaning from the motive behind it. The insight I take from the text is that character is not a fixed thing to be admired or condemned, but a relationship that unfolds through what people want and what they do.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 17–20 mark row. It explains skilfully how qualities, motivations and actions form a loop, and it develops that argument through prejudice and revenge, the caskets, loyalty, belonging and the trial. The references are well chosen and analysed for what they show about the relationship, and the essay stays cohesive from its opening thesis to its closing insight.

sampleAnswers.answer:
In The Merchant of Venice, human qualities, motivations and actions are closely connected, and studying the play has helped me see how a motive can change how a quality is understood. Prejudice is one clear example. Antonio has spat upon Shylock’s “Jewish gaberdine” and called him a dog, so Shylock has a reason to want revenge. When he asks “Hath not a Jew eyes?”, the audience sees a person who feels hurt, and the speech explains why he wants revenge. The action he takes, insisting on the bond, shows that revenge can become cruel.

Money is another motive that links qualities and actions. Bassanio needs money to pursue Portia, so he borrows from Shylock on Antonio’s word. Portia’s suitors choose between caskets, and the Prince of Morocco chooses gold, which is the wrong choice. The lesson that “All that glisters is not gold” shows that appearances can be deceiving. Bassanio chooses the lead casket, which shows humility. His choice is a quality, but he also wants to win Portia, so the quality is connected to a motive.

Loyalty is shown through Antonio, who is willing to die for Bassanio. At the trial he describes himself as “a tainted wether of the flock”, which shows he is ready to accept his fate. This is an example of how a good quality can lead to a dangerous action.

Jessica is another example. She wants to belong to the Christian community, so she leaves her father’s house. She asks what heinous sin it is “To be ashamed to be my father’s child”, which shows that she feels guilt about her own feelings. Shylock’s reaction, as Solanio reports it, “My daughter! O my ducats! O my daughter!”, shows that he loves her but also cares about his money. This shows the link between love and money.

The trial presents mercy as a quality. Portia says “The quality of mercy is not strained”, which suggests that mercy should be freely given. However, her mercy has conditions, and Shylock loses his property. This shows that mercy can be used by people who have power.

In conclusion, studying The Merchant of Venice has shown me that qualities, motivations and actions are connected. Prejudice leads to revenge, love and money are linked, and loyalty can be dangerous. These ideas help me understand that people are complex and that their qualities are shaped by what they want.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 9–12 mark row. It explains several ways in which qualities, motives and actions are connected and supports them with some textual references, including the trial speech and Jessica’s words, with control of language that is adequate but uneven. To reach 13–16, each reference needed to be analysed for its effect rather than paraphrased, and the answer needed to argue how a motive shapes a quality rather than set examples side by side.

sampleAnswers.answer: The Merchant of Venice is a play about Antonio, a merchant who borrows money from Shylock, a moneylender, so that his friend Bassanio can woo Portia. Antonio’s ships are lost at sea, so he cannot repay the loan, and Shylock insists on the bond, which is a pound of flesh. Portia’s father left caskets of gold, silver and lead, and Bassanio chooses the right one and wins her. Later Portia comes to the trial dressed as a lawyer. She says, “The quality of mercy is not strained”, but Shylock refuses to accept her plea. In the end Portia tells the court that the bond allows no blood, and Shylock loses. Jessica, Shylock’s daughter, also runs away with a Christian. The play shows that qualities such as mercy and greed are important to people and that they affect what happens.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 5–8 mark row, at its lower edge. It mostly retells the plot and makes only a brief statement about qualities, with one quotation that is not analysed. To reach 9–12, the answer needed to explain how studying the text has given insight into the relationship between qualities, motivations and actions, and to support that explanation with analysed textual references.

prompts.scenario: Your answer will be assessed on how well you: demonstrate understanding of human experiences in texts; analyse, explain and assess the ways human experiences are represented in texts; organise, develop and express ideas using language appropriate to audience, purpose and context.
prompts.hscSection: Paper 1, Section II — Texts and Human Experiences (20 marks). Allow about 45 minutes.

dotPoints.description: Compose creative and critical texts that affirm or challenge ideas, values and perspectives represented in a range of texts

prompts.question: Construct a creative or critical text that challenges ONE idea, value or perspective represented in a range of texts you have studied, then write a short rationale explaining your choices.
markerNotes: The composed text must do the challenging. A rationale that describes an intention without a text that carries it earns little.
Strong rationales name one or two specific choices in the piece and say why each suits its audience and purpose.
commonStudentErrors: Writing a piece that restates the perspective the task asks them to challenge.
Using a rationale that summarises the plot of the piece instead of explaining the choices.
prompts.markingCriteria:
7-8 marks: Constructs a sustained creative and critical text that challenges ideas, values and perspectives with control of voice and form, and gives a precise rationale linking choices to the texts studied
5-6 marks: Constructs a text that challenges a perspective with clear control, and a rationale that explains some choices
3-4 marks: Constructs a text with a relevant perspective, and a general rationale
1-2 marks: Produces a short text with limited control, and a rationale that describes rather than explains

sampleAnswers.answer:
Composed text: 'The Mill Was Never Ours'

Every council meeting in Harrow Vale begins with the same word: progress. We are told that the new estate on the old mill flats will bring families, jobs and a future. I have walked those flats since I was six. I know where the river used to run, and I know which of the families who sold up never got the chance to return. Progress, in this town, has always been a story told by people who did not have to live with its cost.

The values we call community belong to the ones who stayed. Their trades, their hands and their stubborn gardens made Harrow Vale, and the new brochure does not mention them. A plan that reads only as profit forgets whose labour built the place. So when the planners say the estate is for everyone, I ask: for whom, and at what price? Let us stop calling it a future until we can say who it is for.

Rationale: The column sets out to challenge the perspective that progress is a single good, a view that appears across the council documents and the local texts studied in class. It also challenges the perspectives of council members who treat every change as an improvement, and it does so without naming any one speaker. I chose a first-person opinion voice so the reader meets the argument as a witness rather than a policy claim. The word progress opens and closes the piece, framing it as something contested. The river image is a creative choice that carries the critical point: it asks the reader to picture what was lost, which facts alone would not do. The short paragraphs and rhetorical questions create a critical register that asks the reader to weigh the values on both sides before deciding. A reader who reaches the final question is left to decide which values matter most, which is the critical purpose of the piece.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Full marks: the composed column challenges one perspective (progress as a single good) with a controlled first-person voice and a deliberate frame of repeated words. The rationale explains specific choices (the river image, the opening and closing word, the rhetorical questions) and links them to the texts studied and to the reader's weighing of values, which is the precision the top band asks for.

sampleAnswers.answer:
Composed text: 'Progress for Who?'

The council says the estate is progress. I think it costs too much. The old mill workers would have wanted to stay and see their town kept. Progress should include everyone, not only the new families who are moving in.

Rationale: I wanted to challenge the idea of progress and show a different perspective on the town. I used a short first-person voice because it sounds like a local person.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Five marks: the piece challenges a perspective clearly enough and the voice is controlled, but the text is thin and the rationale explains the intention rather than the choices. The link to the texts studied is absent, which places it in the 5-6 band.

sampleAnswers.answer:
Composed text: a short note that the mill should not be a new estate.

Rationale: I wanted to be creative.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Two marks: the text is short with limited control and the rationale does not explain any choice. The answer produces a text but does not construct a challenge to a perspective.

prompts.scenario: A student is preparing a portfolio for a school publication on civic life. The task asks for an original piece that challenges a perspective commonly found in council documents and local media, followed by a rationale that explains how the piece engages with the texts studied in class. The student's piece is an invented opinion column for a fictional country town, Harrow Vale.

prompts.question: Explain how a text you have studied affirms ONE value while challenging another, using a specific language feature.
markerNotes: Explain the balance. The best answers show that a text can affirm one value and challenge another, and that the language shows which judgement the reader is invited to hold.
Use one specific language feature for each judgement, such as a repeated phrase or a metaphor, and say what it does.
commonStudentErrors: Describing a value that the text affirms without showing a challenge to a different value.
Using 'affirms' and 'challenges' as labels for the whole text instead of for particular choices.
prompts.markingCriteria:
4 marks: Explains how a text affirms and challenges values through specific language, showing how the balance shapes perspective
3 marks: Explains one affirming and one challenging choice with some reference to values
2 marks: Identifies a value that is affirmed or challenged, with brief comment
1 mark: Makes a general comment about the values in the text

sampleAnswers.answer: A text can affirm one value and challenge another, and its language shapes the perspectives that result. In the invented radio feature 'Night Shift at Ferris Cannery', the repeated phrase 'we keep showing up' affirms patient, shared labour, presenting work as a commitment held in common. The metaphor of a government grant as 'a promise written in pencil' challenges the value of quick results. Together these choices create a perspective more complicated than either of the values alone, because the listener must weigh both judgements rather than simply agree or disagree. Readers of texts like this learn to notice that balance, not just the verdict.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Full marks: the explanation shows one affirming choice (the repeated 'we keep showing up') and one challenging choice (the 'promise written in pencil' metaphor), and it explains how the two produce a perspective more complicated than either value alone. The language is traced to the judgements it carries, which is what the top band asks for.

sampleAnswers.answer: The text says we keep showing up, which affirms volunteer work. It also says the grant is written in pencil, which challenges quick results.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Two marks: one affirmed and one challenged value are identified with brief comment. The answer does not explain how the balance between them shapes a perspective.

sampleAnswers.answer: The text has good and bad ideas about the community.
sampleAnswers.feedback: One mark: a general comment is made about values without naming a language feature or a specific value.

prompts.scenario: A debate coach is preparing students to argue that a single text can hold two judgements at once. The student must explain this using the invented radio feature 'Night Shift at Ferris Cannery', which the class has studied. The feature repeats the phrase 'we keep showing up' and describes a government grant as 'a promise written in pencil'.

dotPoints.description: Compose texts using structures, language features and stylistic elements for specific audiences, to reinterpret ideas and perspectives

prompts.question: Construct a short text for a younger audience that reinterprets a perspective from a text you have studied, using structures, language features and stylistic elements, then explain your choices in a brief rationale.
markerNotes: Reinterpreting a perspective means changing whose view organises the text, not only changing the vocabulary. Check that the keeper, not the passenger, holds the central view.
The rationale should name the structural choice first, then the language and stylistic choices that serve the younger audience.
commonStudentErrors: Simplifying the vocabulary but keeping the original passenger's perspective, so nothing is reinterpreted.
Writing a rationale that says the piece is 'for kids' without naming any structure, feature or element.
prompts.markingCriteria:
6 marks: Composes a text that reinterprets a perspective for a specific younger audience, controlling structures, language features and stylistic elements, with a rationale that explains each choice
5 marks: Composes a controlled text for the audience, with a rationale that explains most choices
4 marks: Composes a text with a clear audience and some control of form, with a general rationale
3 marks: Composes a text with some suitable features and a brief rationale
2 marks: Produces a short text with limited control of audience
1 mark: Produces a text with minimal control or a rationale that only restates the task

sampleAnswers.answer:
Composed text: 'The Ferry Keeper's Night'

Every evening the big boat leaves Mollin Cove, and every evening Mr Ansel stays on the jetty to watch it go. Tonight the fog is thick, and the buoy bell rings slow and low, like a question nobody answers.

'Wait for me,' he whispers, though nobody can hear. Someone has to keep the light on for the ones who are still coming home. 'Wait for me,' he says again, and keeps the light on.

Rationale: The piece reinterprets the story's perspectives by reversing the structures of the original. The senior story follows the passenger out of the cove; this one stays on the jetty, so the keeper's waiting organises the text. For a Year 4 audience I used short sentences and a repeated refrain.
