prompts.question: Evaluate how the artistry and integrity of your prescribed text has influenced your understanding of its literary value. In your response, make detailed reference to your prescribed text.
markerNotes: The question asks for an evaluation, so the strongest answers judge how much the text's artistry and integrity contribute to its literary value, rather than listing features the text has.

Artistry and integrity work together. Strong responses show how particular choices of language, structure and form hold the text's ideas together as a whole, and why that coherence matters to its value.
Literary value should be argued, not assumed. The best answers explain what the text offers a reader across contexts and tie that claim to specific moments of craft.
Detailed, well-chosen references across the whole text carry the evaluation. A few passages analysed closely do more than many named in passing.
commonStudentErrors: Listing techniques without explaining how they make the text valuable.
Treating integrity as moral honesty in a character rather than the unity of the text's construction and meaning.
Asserting that the text is a classic as proof of its value, without argument from the text itself.
Retelling the plot or the author's life instead of evaluating the text.
prompts.markingCriteria:
17-20 marks: Evaluates skilfully how the artistry and integrity of the prescribed text has influenced an understanding of its literary value; Demonstrates a well-informed understanding of context, language, form and ideas using well-selected and detailed textual references; Composes an insightful response using language appropriate to audience, purpose and form
13-16 marks: Evaluates effectively how the artistry and integrity of the prescribed text has influenced an understanding of its literary value; Demonstrates an informed understanding of context, language, form and ideas using detailed textual references; Composes an effective response using language appropriate to audience, purpose and form
9-12 marks: Evaluates how the artistry and integrity of the prescribed text has influenced an understanding of its literary value; Demonstrates a sound understanding of context, language, form and ideas using textual references; Composes a sound response using language appropriate to audience, purpose and form
5-8 marks: Describes some aspects of the understanding of the literary value of the prescribed text; Demonstrates some knowledge of the prescribed text with limited textual references; Composes a limited response
1-4 marks: Attempts to describe some aspects of the prescribed text; Attempts to compose a response to the question

sampleAnswers.answer:
The artistry and integrity of Great Expectations are inseparable from its literary value. Dickens's craft gives the novel its memorable images and its shape, while his honesty about Pip's failings keeps those images from becoming decoration. In my view the prescribed text earns its place in the canon because its technique serves a moral vision that the reader can test, rather than because it is merely entertaining. This judgement rests on the retrospective narration, the symbolic house at the centre of the plot, and an ending that refuses to settle the moral account.

The novel's opening sentence, "My father's family name being Pirrip", introduces a narrator who is an adult looking back at a boy he no longer quite is. This retrospective narration is the first sign of artistry. The man can judge the child's snobbery and fear, yet he also remembers those feelings from the inside, so the reader is asked to hold sympathy and distance at once. The technique turns what could be a story of social climbing into a study of how memory edits a life, and that self-scrutiny is where I locate much of the novel's literary value.

Satis House, the home Miss Havisham keeps, is the clearest example of Dickens's symbolic method. It is "a large and dismal house barricaded against robbers", and inside it a watch and a clock have "stopped at twenty minutes to nine". The stopped time is an image of arrested grief, and it is matched by the "withered articles of bridal dress" left to decay. The effect is cumulative because no object is offered as a mere detail; each returns to the same idea of a life frozen after betrayal. This is artistry at its most controlled, and it lifts a melodramatic premise into something the reader feels as a moral condition.

The integrity of the text appears in how Dickens treats Pip's own moral failures. Pip does not merely observe Estella's contempt for his hands; he absorbs it, and the narrator records the moment he becomes "ashamed of my hands". Later the adult Pip admits that he had "deserted Joe", a confession that gives the novel its moral weight. Dickens does not spare Pip through the reveal that Magwitch is his benefactor. Instead Magwitch's pride, "I'm your second father", forces Pip to confront the source of his expectations, and the novel refuses the comfort of a gentleman who is simply good. The value of this honesty is that the reader cannot retreat into an easy verdict on Pip.

The ending is where artistry and integrity meet most sharply. Estella's line "And will continue friends apart" and the closing sentence, in which Pip sees "no shadow of another parting from her", keep the reconciliation within the limits of friendship. The revision matters here: Bulwer-Lytton strongly urged Dickens to change the original ending, and Dickens rewrote it. Whatever the reasons, the final version declines to state a marriage. Readers still argue over whether Pip and Estella are united or merely at peace, and that argument is evidence of literary value, since the novel gives the reader a question rather than a verdict.

I judge the novel's literary value to rest on the tension between its melodramatic machinery and its psychological honesty. Dickens allows comedy into the darkest material, and Wemmick's remark that his elderly father, the Aged, is "in wonderful feather" gives the London chapters a warmth the reader does not expect. These moments do not dilute the moral argument; they make it more persuasive, because the novel's ideas about class and debt are tested against people who take them more lightly as well as against those who suffer.

Taken together, the artistry and integrity of Great Expectations have shaped my understanding of its literary value in a specific way. I first read the novel as a story of ambition, but the narrator's self-judgement, the carefully managed symbols and the open ending transform ambition into a study of guilt and dependence. That transformation, more than the plot, is the source of the text's lasting worth.
sampleAnswers.feedback: This meets the top criteria row: it evaluates how the narration, the symbolic house and the revised ending shape the novel's literary value, and it uses close textual reference throughout. To lift it, the answer could test its judgement against a second reading, such as the novel's humour or a contrary view of the ending.

sampleAnswers.answer:
The artistry and integrity of Great Expectations make it a text with real literary value. Dickens uses a first-person narrator, and the opening line, "My father's family name being Pirrip", shows an adult looking back at himself as a boy. This gives the novel a double view, because the adult can judge the child's behaviour while still remembering how it felt from the inside.

Miss Havisham's house is also important. Satis House is a dismal place, and a watch and a clock have "stopped at twenty minutes to nine". These objects suggest that time has stopped for her after she was betrayed. The bridal dress left to decay supports this idea. I think this is an effective use of symbols, and it makes the novel's melodrama more convincing.

The novel's integrity is shown in Pip's behaviour. Estella criticises his hands, and Pip becomes ashamed of them, which shows how class has changed him. Later he admits that he deserted Joe. Dickens does not hide Pip's faults, and this makes Pip a more believable character.

The ending also shows the text's integrity. Pip and Estella meet again and agree to remain friends, and Pip sees no shadow of another parting. Dickens changed this ending after Bulwer-Lytton urged him to, and readers still disagree about what it means. This uncertainty is one reason the novel has lasting value.

Overall, the artistry and integrity of the prescribed text have shaped my understanding of its literary value. The narration, the symbols and the honest treatment of Pip all make the novel more than a story about a poor boy who becomes a gentleman.
sampleAnswers.feedback: This sits in the middle criteria rows: it is organised and reasonably controlled, but it moves between techniques by describing them and only briefly connects them to literary value. To lift it, choose one technique and argue how it changes the reader's view of Pip's guilt.

sampleAnswers.answer: Great Expectations is a novel by Charles Dickens about a boy called Pip. He lives with his sister and Joe Gargery, and he meets a convict in a churchyard. Later he goes to Miss Havisham's house, which is called Satis House, and he meets Estella. Pip becomes ashamed of his hands and of Joe. At the end he meets Estella again and they agree to be friends. The novel has interesting characters and a strange house with stopped clocks. I think the artistry and integrity of the text make it important. Dickens's writing shows that Pip changes, so the novel has literary value.
sampleAnswers.feedback: This sits in the lowest criteria rows: it summarises the plot and names Satis House and the ending without evaluating them, and it has minimal textual reference. A single quoted line from Miss Havisham's house, used as evidence for a claim about literary value, would begin to meet the stem.

prompts.question: ‘Literature forces us to ask questions and look for answers. Even if those answers do not exist.’ To what extent is this true? In your response, make close reference to your prescribed text.
markerNotes: The question asks for a judgement of the extent to which the statement is true. A response needs a position on that extent, not a description of what the text contains.

The statement has two claims: that literature forces us to ask questions and look for answers, and that those answers may not exist. The strongest responses test each claim and say where the text answers, where it withholds an answer, and what that does to the reader.

A question raised by a text is not the same as an answer it gives. Responses that treat every plot development as an answer, or every open moment as a missing answer, have not evaluated the statement.
Close reference is required throughout. Analyse how language, form and narrative method produce a question or an answer, rather than retelling events as evidence without an argument.
commonStudentErrors: Retelling the plot and treating each event as proof, without deciding whether the text answers the questions it raises.
Stating a position on the statement in the introduction and not returning to it until the conclusion.
Making general claims about literature that could apply to any text, without close reference to the prescribed text.
Assuming that a text which leaves something open has failed to answer, rather than examining what the openness does to the reader.
prompts.markingCriteria:
17-20 marks: Skilfully evaluates the extent to which the statement is true of their prescribed text; Demonstrates a well-informed understanding of context, language, form and ideas using well-selected and detailed textual references; Composes a thoughtful response using language appropriate to audience, purpose and form
13-16 marks: Effectively evaluates the extent to which the statement is true of their prescribed text; Demonstrates an informed understanding of context, language, form and ideas using detailed textual references; Composes an effective response using language appropriate to audience, purpose and form
9-12 marks: Evaluates the extent to which the statement is true of their prescribed text; Demonstrates an understanding of context, language, form and ideas using some textual references; Composes a sound response using language appropriate to audience, purpose and form
5-8 marks: Responds to some aspects of the statement; Demonstrates some understanding of the prescribed text with limited textual references; Composes a limited response
1-4 marks: Attempts to describe aspects of the prescribed text; Attempts to compose a response to the question

sampleAnswers.answer:
Austen’s Emma is, to a considerable extent, a novel that forces its readers to ask questions and then look for answers. The statement is true of it, but its second clause needs qualifying. Emma supplies answers to nearly every puzzle it sets, yet the question on which the novel turns, whether its heroine can see herself clearly, is answered only through the painful experience that her own judgement has produced. The answers exist, but they are harder to reach than the plot first suggests.

The novel invites a question about its heroine from its opening lines. Emma is introduced as “handsome, clever, and rich”, with “a comfortable home and happy disposition” and “very little to distress or vex her”. Such a description makes the reader ask whether a life so untroubled can teach anything at all. The narrator answers within the first chapter: the real evils of Emma’s situation were “having rather too much her own way” and a readiness “to think a little too well of herself”. The answer is given at once, yet the rest of the novel is needed to make it real. Austen’s free indirect style lets Emma’s self-congratulation and the narrator’s irony share a voice, so the reader must keep asking how far the narration can be trusted.

The plot then supplies a sequence of smaller puzzles, and most are answered. Who has sent the pianoforte to Jane Fairfax? Emma suspects Mr Knightley, and the reader is invited to share the suspicion. Why is Jane so reserved, and why does Frank Churchill behave so oddly? Later the novel discloses that Frank has sent the instrument and that he and Jane are secretly engaged. Frank’s attentions to Emma, which she half believes, are part of the concealment. Literature has made us look for answers, and it has supplied them. The same pattern governs Mr Elton. Emma decides that he is in love with Harriet, and his proposal to Emma herself shows how wrong her answer was. Her misreading is not the novel’s failure to answer; it is her failure to accept the answer when it comes.

The more serious questions concern Emma’s judgement of other people, and this is where her answers fail. Harriet, whose parentage is unknown, has no fixed social place, and Emma uses this uncertainty to justify raising her friend’s hopes. She persuades Harriet to refuse Robert Martin, a worthy man whose proposal Emma judges beneath her. The answer to whether Harriet should marry him is available in the text, but Emma cannot see it, because she has settled the question before examining it. Her error is not a lack of information. She has an answer ready before she has looked. Emma’s confidence in her own reading is the very thing that keeps her from testing it.

Box Hill is where the question of Emma’s conduct finally presses on her. Her cruel jibe at Miss Bates is rebuked by Mr Knightley, and his letter afterwards sets out her faults with a plainness she cannot dismiss. Emma reads it and is moved to tears. The tears matter because they show her feeling, rather than reasoning, finally doing the work of judgement. What the letter gives her is an answer she had refused to find for herself, and it comes from the character whose judgement she has most consistently dismissed. The statement assumes that the seeker of answers will also be the finder. Emma shows that an answer can arrive from outside the self before the self is ready to hear it.

The ending gives the reader marriages: Emma and Mr Knightley, Harriet and Robert Martin, Frank and Jane. These answer the questions of plot, and the comic structure delivers them with precision. The marriage of Harriet and Robert Martin confirms what Emma had refused to see. Yet whether Emma has changed for good is not settled by her wedding. Her wealth means that she does not need to marry, so her choice of a husband rests on judgement rather than necessity, and the reader must decide whether that judgement has improved. Austen makes this question unavoidable, and leaves the answer to us.

The statement is therefore largely true of Emma. Literature forces the reader to ask questions, and Austen answers most of them, sometimes through a plot disclosure and sometimes through a letter. But the question on which the novel depends, what Emma is and whether she can truly see, is answered only in the reader’s judgement of her future. Where the text does not state an answer outright, the reader must supply one, and the novel’s power lies in making that work matter.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 17-20 mark row: it skilfully evaluates the extent to which the statement is true of Emma, testing the claim against the novel’s puzzles, Emma’s misreadings and the ending. Its textual references are well-selected and detailed, and each section moves the argument on rather than restating the one before. The conclusion draws the position from the body of the answer.

sampleAnswers.answer:
Austen’s Emma supports the statement to some extent, because the novel asks many questions and many of them are answered. The statement is less convincing in its second part, however, since the answers in the novel are often not the ones Emma expects, and the most important answer is left to the reader.

The early chapters give the reader a clear picture of Emma. She is handsome, clever and rich, and the narrator says she has very little to distress her. This makes the reader wonder what Emma could learn. The narrator also names her chief faults as having too much her own way and thinking too well of herself, so the question of her character is answered early, although Emma does not accept the answer. The reader is therefore aware of Emma’s flaws from the beginning of the novel, which makes the later events easier to follow.

Many of the mysteries in the novel are solved in the end. Emma thinks Mr Knightley has sent the pianoforte to Jane Fairfax, but it is Frank Churchill who has sent it. Frank and Jane are also secretly engaged, which explains his behaviour. Mr Elton, whom Emma believes is in love with Harriet, proposes to Emma herself. These are answers to questions the novel asks, and they show that literature gives us answers as well as questions. The reader can see where Emma’s guesses go wrong, which keeps the reading active.

Emma’s misjudgement of Harriet is more serious. Emma persuades Harriet to refuse Robert Martin’s proposal, and Harriet later marries him, which shows that the answer was there from the start. Emma did not look for it. This part of the novel supports the statement, because the answer exists even though Emma cannot see it. Her view of Harriet’s social position is also important, because she wants her friend to marry above her station, and this shapes every choice she makes for Harriet.

At Box Hill, Emma insults Miss Bates, and Mr Knightley rebukes her. Afterwards he writes a letter pointing out her faults, especially her unkindness to Miss Bates. Emma reads the letter and feels deep regret. The letter gives her an answer to her own question about her behaviour, and it shows that answers can come from other people. This episode supports the first part of the statement, since the answer arrives from outside Emma.

The novel ends with marriages. Emma marries Mr Knightley, Harriet marries Robert Martin, and Frank marries Jane. These answer the questions of the plot. However, the reader has to decide whether Emma has changed, because the novel does not state this directly. In this way the novel leaves an open question at the end, and the reader must answer it.

In conclusion, the statement is true to some extent. Emma asks many questions and gives many answers, but the most important answer is about Emma herself, and the novel does not fully give it. The reader must work it out.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 9-12 mark row: it evaluates the extent to which the statement is true of Emma and uses some textual references, but the plot is retold more often than it is analysed, and the conclusion repeats earlier points without developing them. To reach 13, each plot point needed a technique or a specific moment that tested the claim about answers, rather than being cited as proof of it.

sampleAnswers.answer: In Emma, the heroine is always trying to find answers. She thinks Mr Elton likes Harriet, but he proposes to Emma instead. She thinks Mr Knightley sent the pianoforte, but it was Frank Churchill. The novel gives answers to these questions, so the statement is true. Emma also gets an answer from Mr Knightley’s letter after Box Hill, which tells her she was rude to Miss Bates. Those answers are all clear, which makes the statement easy to agree with. The ending gives everyone a marriage, which answers who ends up with whom. Some people might say the answers do not exist, but I think the novel has answers for most things. So the statement is mostly true.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 5-8 mark row: it responds to some aspects of the statement and gives limited textual reference, mostly to plot events. It does not evaluate the extent to which the statement is true, and it dismisses the second clause in a single sentence. To reach 9, the answer needed to weigh whether the novel’s answers are complete and to support that judgement with a specific moment from Emma.

prompts.question: Evaluate how your personal and intellectual engagement with your prescribed text has been intensified by its construction. In your response, make detailed reference to your prescribed text.
markerNotes: The question asks how an engagement has been intensified by construction. Responses must name the engagement, personal, intellectual or both, and then identify the particular structural or formal choices that intensify it.

Construction covers structure, sequencing, shifts between modes, direct address to the audience and the handling of parallel situations. The best answers select two or three of these and trace each to a specific moment in the text.

Personal engagement is the pull of the text on the reader’s feelings and loyalties. Intellectual engagement is the judgement the text forces the reader to make. Answers that treat these as the same thing rarely evaluate the question.
Detailed reference is stipulated by the question. Quote briefly and accurately, and analyse what each choice makes the reader feel or think, rather than what it contains.
commonStudentErrors: Describing the structure of the text without explaining how that structure draws the reader in.
Confusing personal engagement with enjoyment of the text, or intellectual engagement with a summary of its ideas.
Naming a technique such as contrast, soliloquy or foreshadowing without linking it to a particular moment or to the reader’s response.
Asserting that the construction intensifies engagement without showing how the reader’s position changes between one part of the text and another.
prompts.markingCriteria:
17-20 marks: Evaluates skilfully how their personal and intellectual engagement with their prescribed text has been intensified by its construction; Demonstrates a well-informed understanding of context, language, form and ideas using well-selected and detailed textual references as stipulated in the question; Composes an insightful response using language appropriate to audience, purpose and form
13-16 marks: Evaluates effectively how their personal and intellectual engagement with their prescribed text has been intensified by its construction; Demonstrates an informed understanding of context, language, form and ideas using detailed textual references as stipulated in the question; Composes an effective response using language appropriate to audience, purpose and form
9-12 marks: Evaluates how their personal and intellectual engagement with their prescribed text has been intensified by its construction; Demonstrates a sound understanding of context, language, form and ideas using textual references as stipulated in the question; Composes a sound response using language appropriate to audience, purpose and form
5-8 marks: Responds to some aspects of the question; Demonstrates some knowledge of the prescribed text with limited textual references; Composes a limited response
1-4 marks: Attempts to describe aspects of the prescribed text; Attempts to compose a response to the question

sampleAnswers.answer:
King Henry IV, Part 1 intensifies both my personal and my intellectual engagement through its construction, and the two effects depend on each other. The play draws me in by making me a confidant of its central figure. It holds me back by refusing to let any one world, whether court, tavern or battlefield, settle how a prince should live. The engagement is therefore more than enjoyment. It is a continuing act of judgement, and the play’s shaping makes that judgement unavoidable.

The personal engagement begins with the soliloquy in which Prince Hal speaks alone to the audience. He tells us that he will for a time uphold, in his companions, “the unyoked humour of your idleness”, and he explains that he will “make offence a skill” so that his reform will shine the more when it comes. Because he confides in us, I become his accomplice. The speech is a pleasure in itself: the rhythm is confident, the couplets are neat, and I am invited to admire a plan I have not yet been asked to approve. That invitation makes the rest of the play personal, because we have already taken Hal’s side.

The play then moves straight to Eastcheap, where Falstaff speaks in loose, witty prose and the company at the Boar’s Head seems to exist for its own amusement. The shift from the rhymed verse of the prince’s confession to the prose of the tavern draws me into Falstaff’s company as Hal is drawn, and the crew’s plan to rob travellers at Gadshill soon makes their pleasures look like crimes. The comedy keeps me laughing, and the plan keeps me uneasy. The construction holds personal pleasure and moral unease in the same scene.

The intellectual engagement is intensified by the parallels the construction creates. The king’s rebuke of Hal, which measures the prince against Hotspur, sets the two young men side by side. Hal answers by promising to “be more myself”, and the audience must test that promise against the Eastcheap scenes it has just watched. Hotspur’s ambition is stated in heroic verse, as he will “pluck bright honour from the pale-faced moon”, and he turns danger to advantage with the same energy, plucking safety from danger as if from a nettle. We can admire that energy, but the play also shows its recklessness. Hal, by contrast, has spent the early scenes in Eastcheap, so the audience must decide whether his idleness is a fault or a strategy. The play gives evidence for both readings, and it keeps the two men in counterpoint so that every court scene sends us back to the question of what honour is worth.

The construction also tests claims against results. Glendower boasts that he can “call spirits from the vasty deep”, and Hotspur replies with dry scepticism, “Why, so can I”, asking whether those spirits will come when they are called. The exchange is comic, but it asks what makes a claim believable, and that question returns at Shrewsbury. The battle sequence makes it sharper. Falstaff’s catechism on honour asks “What is honour? A word”, and so ridicules the heroic rhetoric we have just been admiring. The audience must hold the comic and the serious together. At Shrewsbury, Falstaff feigns death to save himself and then claims to have killed Hotspur. His excuse, that “The better part of valour is discretion”, is a joke the audience has been trained to enjoy, so it is hard to reject and hard to accept.

When Hal kills Hotspur and speaks his epitaph, “Fare thee well, great heart”, the honour he has earned is real. Falstaff then claims the kill. The construction places these two claims side by side, so that the battlefield becomes a test of reputation: what a man has done and what he is credited with doing. The play gives us the joke and the lie together, and it does not tell us which should prevail. The moment is brief, but it asks the audience to decide quickly whether it admires the prince, the knight or the joke.

The construction intensifies engagement because it keeps the audience a double witness. We see Hal’s private plan beside his public deeds, and we see Falstaff’s private cowardice beside his public boasts. Each pairing asks us to set what a character says in private against what he does in public. The personal pull of the tavern and the intellectual demand of the court are never allowed to resolve into one. Hal’s promise to be more himself is not settled within this play, so the judgement of his reform remains with the audience when the final battle is over.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 17-20 mark row: it skilfully evaluates how personal and intellectual engagement have been intensified by the construction of King Henry IV, Part 1, and it keeps the two forms of engagement distinct. Its detailed references, to the soliloquy, the alternation of court and tavern, the parallel between Hal and Hotspur and the battlefield reversal, are well-selected, and the argument is sustained across the whole answer.

sampleAnswers.answer:
King Henry IV, Part 1 engages the audience both personally and intellectually, and its construction helps to strengthen this engagement, although not in every part of the play. The most noticeable feature is the way the play moves between different groups of characters, so that attention is always shifting. This helps the audience follow more than one story at once, and it keeps the audience from settling into any one world.

At the start, Prince Hal speaks directly to the audience. He tells us that he is spending time with low company but that he has a plan. He says he will offend people so that his reform will look better later, and he uses the phrase “make offence a skill”. Because he tells us his plan, the audience feels trusted and involved. This is an example of how the play engages the audience personally, and it makes the audience part of the scheme. The soliloquy is also quite short, but it sets up the rest of the play.

The play then goes to the tavern, where Falstaff is. Falstaff is funny and his speech is loose and humorous. The comedy makes the audience enjoy being in his company, and the play also shows the gang planning to rob travellers at Gadshill. This contrast between comedy and crime makes the audience think about the characters’ behaviour, so the engagement becomes intellectual as well as personal. The audience can see that the tavern is fun but not entirely harmless.

The construction also places Hal and Hotspur next to each other. Hotspur is brave and talks about honour, and he says he will pluck honour from the moon. Hal is in the tavern, so the audience has to decide which of them is the better model. The king also compares the two young men, and this comparison is clear to the audience. The play presents both characters in a way that encourages comparison, which makes the audience think about what honour means and whether it can be trusted.

Falstaff also talks about honour. He says honour is only a word, which makes the heroic talk of the battle seem less serious. At the battle, Falstaff pretends to be dead and then claims he killed Hotspur, even though Hal killed him. This shows the difference between what people do and what they are credited with doing, and it makes the audience question the reputation of the characters. The ending of the battle scene is therefore important to the way the audience reads the whole play.

In conclusion, the construction of King Henry IV, Part 1 makes the audience engage with the characters and think about honour. The play uses comedy and the battle to keep the audience interested, and it leaves the question of Hal’s reform open at the end.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 9-12 mark row: it explains some features of the construction and how they engage the audience, but it describes more than it evaluates, and its references are some rather than detailed. The personal and intellectual forms of engagement are not separated. To reach 13, each paragraph needed to name a structural choice, quote the moment that carries it and explain its effect on the audience’s judgement.

sampleAnswers.answer: Prince Hal spends time in a tavern with Falstaff and tells the audience he is doing it on purpose. The play then goes to the battle, where Hal fights Hotspur and kills him. Falstaff pretends to be dead and then says that he killed Hotspur. This makes the audience think the play is both funny and serious. Hal talking to the audience makes the audience involved in his plan, so the play is engaging in a personal way. It also makes the audience think about honour and whether Hal is an honourable person. The construction makes the audience feel close to the characters. The audience also thinks the play is clever because it has both comedy and battles.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 5-8 mark row: it responds to some aspects of the question and retells events from the tavern and the battle, with limited textual reference. It does not evaluate how the engagement has been intensified by construction, and no structural feature is named as the cause. To reach 9, the answer needed to name one feature of construction, such as the soliloquy, and explain how it draws the audience in.

prompts.question: Explain how the language of critical expression refines arguments and interprets texts in a critical study.
markerNotes: The question asks how, so the answer must show the mechanism. Naming critical terms without showing what they do earns little.
A good answer shows that refining an argument means qualifying a claim against evidence, not simply adding detail.
Examples should be specific to the text and show the link between technique and effect.
commonStudentErrors: Uses everyday words such as 'sad' or 'good' and does not show the difference the critical vocabulary makes.
Explains terms in general without applying them to a critical study of a text.
prompts.markingCriteria:
6 marks: Explains in detail how specific critical terms refine arguments and interpret texts, linking each term to its effect on the reading, with well-chosen evidence
5 marks: Explains how the language of critical expression refines arguments and interprets texts, with a clear example
4 marks: Explains the function of critical language in refining arguments, with some development
3 marks: Describes critical terms and gives a general statement of their function
2 marks: Identifies critical terms with limited explanation
1 mark: Makes a relevant but unsupported comment

sampleAnswers.answer: The language of critical expression works by making a claim precise and then testing it against the text. A student does not simply say that a novel is sad; they name the emotion, specify where it is produced and state the technique responsible. This precision refines arguments because every general claim must be qualified by evidence. A claim that the novel is isolating, for example, can be refined by showing that its narrow, interior narration and recurring images of closed doors make isolation a structural feature rather than a theme alone. The same vocabulary interprets texts by linking technique to effect, so the reader sees how a device produces a response. Terms such as juxtaposition, implication and qualification let a critical study move from observation to interpretation without losing rigour. The language of critical expression is therefore not decoration. It separates a reasoned reading from a personal reaction, because each sentence must justify itself through textual evidence.
sampleAnswers.feedback: The answer explains the mechanism, not just the vocabulary: a claim is qualified by evidence, and the technique is linked to its effect. The worked example shows the refinement in action, so it earns full marks.

sampleAnswers.answer: The language of critical expression makes claims more exact. A student who writes that a novel is isolating must say what creates the isolation, such as the narrow focus of the narration. This refines arguments because the claim has to be backed by evidence. It also interprets texts by linking a technique to the effect it has on the reader, which is what a critical study requires.
sampleAnswers.feedback: The function of the language is explained with one example, but the answer does not develop several terms or show the refinement in stages, so it sits in the 4-mark band.

sampleAnswers.answer: The language of critical expression helps the student write a better essay about the text.
sampleAnswers.feedback: A relevant comment with no explanation of how the language refines or interprets. This is the 1-mark standard.

prompts.scenario: A Year 12 student is drafting a critical study of an invented novel, written for this task, and wants to show how precise language turns an opinion into a reasoned argument. The teacher has asked for the language of critical expression to be used, not everyday speech. Its narration is narrow and interior, with recurring images of closed doors.

prompts.question: Define the term 'interpretation' as it is used in the language of critical expression.
markerNotes: A definition needs to be precise. Saying an interpretation is 'what you think' is not enough.
The best answers connect the definition to the function of the term within a critical study.
Students should avoid defining the word using the word itself.
commonStudentErrors: Defines interpretation as 'an opinion' or 'what the text means to you', which misses the reasoned and evidenced nature of the term.
Gives a definition that is correct but ignores the critical study context.
prompts.markingCriteria:
2 marks: Gives a precise definition that identifies an interpretation as a reasoned claim about meaning, supported by textual evidence, and refers to how an argument is refined
1 mark: Gives a general definition that does not refer to evidence or to the function of an argument

sampleAnswers.answer: In the language of critical expression, an interpretation is a reasoned claim about what a text means and how its techniques create that meaning, supported by textual evidence. It refines an argument by moving beyond what happens in the text.
sampleAnswers.feedback: The definition is precise: it names the reasoned claim, the evidence and the function of the term in refining an argument. This earns both marks.

sampleAnswers.answer: An interpretation is what you think the text means.
sampleAnswers.feedback: A general definition that treats the term as a personal opinion and does not refer to evidence. This is the 1-mark standard.

prompts.scenario: A glossary for a critical study unit must give students a precise meaning for the term 'interpretation' before they apply it to an invented novel written for this task.

dotPoints.description: The ways mode, medium and form shape and inform responses to texts

prompts.question: Examine the ways mode, medium and form shape and inform responses to a text.
markerNotes: Examining means looking closely at how each element works, so the answer should separate mode, medium and form rather than treating them as one idea.
The comparison between the printed and staged versions is the strongest route to a top-band answer, because it shows the elements producing different responses.
Responses should be tied to the audience's experience, such as what the reader can see or imagine.
commonStudentErrors: Uses mode, medium and form as synonyms, so the three elements are not distinguished.
Describes the adaptation's plot without linking any element to the audience's response.
prompts.markingCriteria:
6 marks: Examines in detail how mode, medium and form shape and inform responses, comparing the effect of each element on the audience, with precise evidence
5 marks: Examines how mode, medium and form shape responses, with clear examples of their effects
4 marks: Explains how mode, medium and form affect responses, with some development of one element
3 marks: Describes mode, medium and form and gives a general statement of their effect on responses
2 marks: Identifies the elements with limited explanation
1 mark: Makes a relevant but unsupported comment

sampleAnswers.answer: Mode is the broad channel through which the story reaches its audience. The printed novel is written, so the reader constructs the setting and voices privately, which makes the responses intimate and inward. The stage adaptation is spoken and visual, so the audience receives the story in real time, shared with others in the room. Medium refines this difference. Print carries the narrator's thoughts directly on the page, while the stage relies on actors' bodies, lighting and silence, so the same grief can be felt as a private confession in one version and a public display in the other. Form then helps shape what the audience expects. The novel's chapters allow pauses and rereading, which lets the reader hold back judgement, whereas the play's scenes move the audience forward and create pressure to respond at once. Taken together, the three elements make the printed novel an intimate experience and the stage adaptation a collective one, so the same story produces different responses.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Each element is separated and linked to a specific effect on the audience, and the comparison between the two versions makes the examination concrete. The answer shows that the elements shape and inform responses, which is what the top band needs.

sampleAnswers.answer: The printed novel is a written mode, so the reader constructs the setting privately and the response is inward. The stage adaptation is a spoken and visual mode, which means the audience sees and hears the story together. The medium is different as well, because print carries the narrator's thoughts directly while the stage relies on actors and lighting. These differences change how the grief in the story is received, since the reader may feel it as a confession and the audience as a public display.
sampleAnswers.feedback: The three elements are separated and their effect on the response is explained, but only one element is developed in detail, so the answer sits in the 4-mark band.

sampleAnswers.answer: A play and a novel are different, so people react to them differently.
sampleAnswers.feedback: A relevant observation with no examination of mode, medium or form. This is the 1-mark standard.

prompts.scenario: A film studies class compares a printed short novel with a stage adaptation of the same invented story, both written for this task. Students must consider how mode, medium and form shape the audience's response to each version.

prompts.question: Identify two differences between mode and medium as they are used to shape responses to a text.
markerNotes: Two differences are required. Mode is the broad channel of communication; medium is the specific material or technology that carries it.
The strongest answers connect each difference to a response, not just a definition.
Accuracy matters more than length in a recall question.
commonStudentErrors: Gives two definitions of mode and medium without any difference between them.
Confuses medium with genre, so the answer describes the text type rather than the carrier.
prompts.markingCriteria:
2 marks: Identifies two accurate differences between mode and medium, and links at least one to the form or response of the text
1 mark: Identifies one accurate difference, or a general difference without reference to response

sampleAnswers.answer: Mode is the broad channel of communication, such as written or spoken, and it shapes the responses a reader has to a text. Medium is the specific material that carries the text, and it changes how the form is experienced.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Two accurate differences are identified, and each is linked to the response of the audience and the form of the text. This earns both marks.

sampleAnswers.answer: Mode is how a text communicates, while medium is what carries it.
sampleAnswers.feedback: One accurate difference with no link to response. This is the 1-mark standard.

prompts.scenario: A Year 12 class is revising the terms used to describe how texts reach their audiences, before applying them to a short invented story written for this task.

dotPoints.description: The ways language forms, features and structures are used to represent a range of perspectives

prompts.question: Explain how language forms, features and structures are used to represent a range of perspectives in the novel.
markerNotes: The question asks how the three elements work together, so the best answers show the interaction between form, language and structure rather than treating each in isolation.
Representing perspectives means showing how each voice is made distinct and how the reader is positioned in relation to it.
Examples from the invented novel should be specific, such as the difference in sentence length between narrator and witnesses.
commonStudentErrors: Lists the forms in the novel without saying which perspective each one represents.
Treats language features and structure as the same thing, so the answer does not separate them.
prompts.markingCriteria:
6 marks: Explains in detail how language forms, features and structures work together to represent a range of perspectives, with precise evidence for each
5 marks: Explains how two of the three elements represent perspectives, with clear examples
4 marks: Explains how forms, language and structure represent perspectives, with some development of one element
3 marks: Describes forms, language features and structures, with a general statement of their effect on perspectives
2 marks: Identifies relevant elements with limited explanation
1 mark: Makes a relevant but unsupported comment

sampleAnswers.answer: Language forms, features and structures work together in the invented novel to represent a range of perspectives, and each layer contributes something the others cannot. At the level of form, the novel alternates between the clerk's first-person account, official court transcripts and letters from witnesses, so the reader receives the same trial as a series of partial accounts. Each form carries its own authority: the transcript claims objectivity, the letters claim intimacy, and the clerk's narration claims a privileged view that the other documents gradually undermine. Language features reinforce these differences. The clerk's sentences are long and qualified, which signals an anxious attempt to be fair, while the witnesses use short, emotionally charged statements that resist qualification. The structure then arranges these perspectives so that the reader meets the official record before the personal testimony, and the sequence itself suggests which voice the novel expects to be trusted. Yet the final chapter reverses this expectation by placing a witness's letter after the clerk's confident conclusion, forcing the reader to reconsider everything before it. The novel therefore represents a range of perspectives not by stating them but by building a structure in which each perspective is tested against the others. The reader is left to weigh them, which is the central effect the form is designed to produce.
sampleAnswers.feedback: The three elements are explained together, each with specific evidence, and the answer shows how the structure tests the perspectives against one another. This is the detailed, interacting explanation the top band requires.

sampleAnswers.answer: The novel uses different forms, such as the clerk's narration and the court transcripts, so the trial is told in several ways. The language also changes, because the clerk writes long sentences while the witnesses use short ones. The structure puts the official record first and the personal testimony later, which shapes how the reader sees the trial. These choices let the novel show different perspectives on the same event.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Forms, language and structure are all identified and linked to perspectives, but the explanation of how each one represents a perspective is brief and only one element is developed, so this sits in the 4-mark band.

sampleAnswers.answer: The novel has different types of writing in it, which show different people's views.
sampleAnswers.feedback: A relevant comment with no explanation of how any element works. This is the 1-mark standard.

prompts.scenario: A stylistics unit asks students to examine an invented novel, written for this task, whose narrator is a court clerk reporting the same trial through several documents. Students must explain how the novel's language and form give voice to a range of perspectives. The documents include court transcripts, letters from witnesses and the clerk's own narration. The final chapter is a witness's letter that follows the clerk's confident conclusion.

prompts.question: Interpret how the structure of the play represents a range of perspectives on a single event.
markerNotes: Interpreting asks for meaning, not description. The answer should say what the structure makes the audience understand.
The ordering of the monologues is the strongest evidence here, because it shows how the play positions each perspective.
Language features should be used to show the social position of each speaker, not just listed.
commonStudentErrors: Describes each monologue in turn without interpreting how the sequence affects the audience.
Says the play 'shows different views' without explaining how the structure makes them available to the audience.
prompts.markingCriteria:
4 marks: Interprets in detail how the structure and language features of the play represent a range of perspectives on the event, with precise evidence
3 marks: Interprets how the structure represents perspectives, with a clear example
2 marks: Describes the structure and perspectives with limited interpretation
1 mark: Makes a relevant but unsupported comment

sampleAnswers.answer: The structure of the play represents a range of perspectives by refusing to privilege any one of them. Four monologues recount the same factory fire, and their accounts overlap and contradict one another, so the audience holds several versions at once. The language features mark each speaker's social position: the foreman's clipped, managerial sentences, the young worker's fragmented emotion and the investigator's measured detachment. The ordering then shapes how the audience weighs them. Placing the foreman first gives his version the authority of a first account, which the later monologues gradually erode. The play thus interprets one event through many voices that the audience must reconcile.
sampleAnswers.feedback: The answer interprets rather than describes: it explains what the sequence and the varied language do to the audience's judgement. The point about the foreman's first account is a precise interpretive move, so it earns full marks.

sampleAnswers.answer: The play has four monologues, so it shows different people's views of the fire. The speakers use different language, which shows their social positions.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Structure and language are described, but the answer does not interpret how the audience is positioned to weigh the perspectives. This is the 2-mark band.

sampleAnswers.answer: The play uses different characters to tell the story.
sampleAnswers.feedback: A description of one feature with no interpretation. This is the 1-mark standard.

prompts.scenario: An invented play, written for this task, presents the same night of a factory fire through four monologues, each delivered by a different character. Students are asked to interpret how the play's structure allows the audience to hold several perspectives at once. The speakers are a foreman, a young worker, an outside investigator and a night guard, and the foreman speaks first.

dotPoints.description: The ways texts can reflect, confirm and challenge expectations associated with particular genres and styles

prompts.question: Discuss the ways texts reflect, confirm and challenge expectations associated with particular genres and styles.
markerNotes: Discuss requires considering more than one side. The strongest answers show where the text meets a genre expectation and where it breaks one, and what each does for the reader.
Style is a separate line of evidence from plot. A top answer treats the prose style and the genre conventions as two things that can confirm or challenge each other.
Genre expectations should be named precisely, such as the reader's trust that clues are fair and the solution will arrive.
commonStudentErrors: Summarises the plot and says it is 'typical of the genre' without identifying which expectation is met or broken.
Discusses only confirmation or only challenge, so the answer does not weigh both.
prompts.markingCriteria:
7-8 marks: Discusses in sustained detail how the text reflects, confirms and challenges genre expectations and styles, with well-chosen evidence and a clear view of the effect on readers
5-6 marks: Discusses how the text reflects and challenges expectations associated with its genre, with relevant evidence that is not fully developed
4 marks: Identifies reflection and challenge with one example each and limited discussion of styles
2-3 marks: Describes features of the genre with a general comment on expectations
1 mark: Makes a relevant but unsupported comment

sampleAnswers.answer: Texts reflect, confirm and challenge the expectations associated with particular genres and styles in ways that reveal how readers are trained to read. The invented detective novel in this scenario reflects its genre most clearly in its puzzle structure: a crime is committed in the first chapter, a list of suspects is assembled, and the reader is invited to solve the mystery alongside the detective. These conventions confirm the reader's expectation that the text will be ordered, that clues will be fair and that the solution will arrive in the final chapter. The styles of the prose also confirm the genre, since its clipped, observational sentences echo the hardboiled tradition that readers associate with the form. Yet the novel challenges expectations in its narrative voice. The narrator is a suspect, and the detective's rational account is undermined by fragments of a diary that the genre would normally treat as irrelevant. This challenge reflects a broader change in how genre is practised: the reader who expects a reassuring solution is left uncertain about whether justice has been achieved. The novel also draws on a second style, the fragmented, interior narration more often associated with literary fiction, and this blend challenges the boundaries of the genre without abandoning its pleasures. Ultimately, the text both reflects and resists the expectations of its genres, and its effect depends on the reader's familiarity with those expectations. A text that only confirms its genre offers comfort, while one that challenges it asks the reader to reconsider what the genre is for. Read this way, the novel's challenge to its genre is not a rejection of the form but a conversation with its readers about what the form has always promised.
sampleAnswers.feedback: The answer discusses both confirmation and challenge, uses evidence from structure, voice and prose style, and states the effect on the reader. Each of the six keywords is used in an argument, which the top band requires.

sampleAnswers.answer: The detective novel reflects its genre through its puzzle structure, because a crime is committed early and the reader is asked to solve it. This confirms what readers expect from the genre. However, the narrator is a suspect and the diary fragments challenge the expectation of a rational solution. So the text both reflects and challenges its genre, and this makes readers think about what the genre usually offers.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Reflection and challenge are both discussed with one example each and a conclusion, but the discussion of style and the wider purpose of the genre is thin. This fits the 5-6 band.

sampleAnswers.answer: The novel is a detective story, so it follows the rules of the genre and has a mystery.
sampleAnswers.feedback: The genre is named and the answer comments on it, but expectations and style are not discussed. This is the 2-3 mark band at its lower end.

prompts.scenario: A critical essay asks students to discuss how the invented detective novel in this scenario, written for this task, relates to the conventions of its genre. The novel follows a classic puzzle structure but uses a fragmented narrative voice more typical of a different style. The novel opens with a crime, a list of suspects and a narrator who is also a suspect, and it includes diary fragments. Its sentences are clipped and observational, and the detective's rational account is undermined by the diary fragments.

prompts.question: Contrast the ways the two texts confirm and challenge the expectations of their genres.
markerNotes: Contrast means setting the two texts against each other. A strong answer shows the opposite choices and the different response each one asks for.
The effect on the reader is what makes the contrast meaningful, so name what each text asks the reader to feel or do.
Avoid writing two separate descriptions joined by 'however'; the comparison should be built into each sentence.
commonStudentErrors: Describes the detective story and the romance separately, with no direct comparison.
Says one text is 'good' and the other is 'bad' rather than explaining how each uses its genre.
prompts.markingCriteria:
5 marks: Contrasts in detail how each text confirms or challenges genre expectations, and explains the effect on the reader with precise evidence
4 marks: Contrasts the two texts with clear examples of confirmation and challenge
3 marks: Identifies one way each text confirms or challenges expectations, with brief explanation
2 marks: Describes one text's genre conventions with limited comparison
1 mark: Makes a relevant but unsupported comment

sampleAnswers.answer: The two texts confirm and challenge the expectations of their genres in opposite directions. The detective story confirms its genre by keeping the puzzle intact: clues arrive in order, the reader has the same information as the detective, and the solution restores order. The romance, by contrast, challenges the genre. Its meeting, misunderstanding and reconciliation follow convention, yet the reconciliation is refused, so the reader must reconsider what the genre promises. Where the detective story rewards the reader for expecting the familiar, the romance turns that expectation into a critical question. Both texts therefore use genre to engage the reader, but in opposite ways: one reassures, the other withholds. One text invites comfort; the other invites scrutiny of the form itself.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Each text is set against the other, and the effect on the reader is explained for both. The comparison is built into the sentences, which is what distinguishes the top band.

sampleAnswers.answer: The detective story keeps the puzzle structure, so it confirms the genre. The romance does not give the happy ending the reader expects, so it challenges the genre. The reader expects different things from each text.
sampleAnswers.feedback: One confirmation and one challenge are identified, but the answer does not explain how each text's conventions produce the effect on the reader. This is the 3-mark band.

sampleAnswers.answer: One text follows its genre and the other does not.
sampleAnswers.feedback: A general contrast with no evidence or effect. This is the 1-mark standard.

prompts.scenario: A literature class has read two short texts written for this task: a detective story that keeps the genre's puzzle structure, and a romance that subverts the genre's happy ending. The romance follows a meeting, a misunderstanding and a reconciliation that is refused. Students must contrast how each text confirms or challenges the reader's expectations of its genre.

dotPoints.description: The ways context can shape social, moral and ethical perspectives in texts

prompts.question: Analyse how the context of the story shapes its social, moral and ethical perspectives.
markerNotes: Analysis means showing the mechanism: how a specific feature of the context produces a specific perspective.
Strong answers link the social context to the moral position, not just list them side by side.
The reader's position matters too: the story presents perspectives that the reader is invited to weigh.
commonStudentErrors: Describes the drought and the town without showing how either shapes a value held by the characters.
Uses 'context' as a label for setting but does not link it to a perspective.
prompts.markingCriteria:
6 marks: Analyses in detail how context shapes social, moral and ethical perspectives, with linked evidence and clear consequences for the story's values
5 marks: Analyses the link between context and at least two perspectives, with specific evidence
4 marks: Analyses how context shapes one perspective, with some development
3 marks: Describes the context and a perspective with a general link
2 marks: Identifies the context or a perspective with limited analysis
1 mark: Makes a relevant but unsupported comment

sampleAnswers.answer:
The context of the story shapes its social, moral and ethical perspectives by determining what the characters can afford to value. The drought is the central fact of the setting, and it shapes the town's social hierarchy: boat owners can wait out the dry season, while labourers depend on daily wages that disappear with the catch. This social context makes the moral perspective uneasy from the outset, because generosity costs each family something different.

The ethical perspectives emerge from that pressure. When the labourer's son steals food in the hungry months, the story does not condemn him outright, since hunger makes the act understandable, yet it does not excuse the theft either. The moral position is shaped by necessity rather than abstract principle. The long drought gives this historical context its force, because it makes survival the pressing concern. Context therefore does not simply surround the perspectives; it shapes them, making the reader weigh obligation against need in every scene. The story leaves that tension unresolved, so the reader must judge whether the town's values were fair.
sampleAnswers.feedback: The answer analyses the mechanism: the drought shapes the social hierarchy, which shapes the moral position, which is then tested by a specific episode. Each keyword is used in an argument, so it earns full marks.

sampleAnswers.answer: The drought shapes the town's social context, because the boat owners can wait it out but the labourers cannot. This makes the moral perspective uneasy, since generosity means different things to different families. The son's theft is not condemned outright because hunger is part of the context, so the story's ethical position depends on circumstance.
sampleAnswers.feedback: The link between context and one perspective is analysed with a specific example, but the analysis is not developed further and the historical context is not used, so this sits in the 4-mark band.

sampleAnswers.answer: The drought affects the people in the town, so they have different views.
sampleAnswers.feedback: A relevant comment about the setting with no analysis of perspective. This is the 1-mark standard.

prompts.scenario: A social studies teacher gives students an invented short story, written for this task, set in a fishing town during a long drought. Students must analyse how the historical and social context shapes the moral and ethical perspectives that the story presents. Boat owners can wait out the dry season, while labourers depend on daily wages, and one labourer's son steals food in the hungry months.

prompts.question: Demonstrate how ONE ethical perspective in the story is shaped by the town's economic context.
markerNotes: Demonstrate means showing the link through a worked example. The episode should carry the argument, not sit beside it.
The best responses show that the perspective is tested by the pressure of the context rather than simply existing in the story.
Name the perspective precisely, such as loyalty to the crew, rather than writing 'the ethics of the story'.
commonStudentErrors: Names an ethical perspective but does not connect it to economic pressure.
Describes an episode without saying what it shows about the perspective.
prompts.markingCriteria:
4 marks: Demonstrates clearly, using a specific episode, how the economic context shapes the ethical perspective, with precise reasoning
3 marks: Demonstrates the link between economic pressure and the perspective, with an example
2 marks: Identifies the perspective and a feature of the context, with limited reasoning
1 mark: Makes a relevant but unsupported comment

sampleAnswers.answer: One ethical perspective in the story is that loyalty to the crew matters more than individual gain. The economic context has shaped it: when the boats cannot go out in the drought, the owners reduce wages. The episode in which the older fisherman refuses to sell his share of the catch demonstrates the point. His refusal is not naive, because in a town where the drought makes the catch a matter of survival, loyalty becomes a practical strategy as well as a moral value. The ethical perspective is therefore tested by the pressure of the town's economy, and it endures.
sampleAnswers.feedback: The perspective is named precisely, the economic context is explained, and the fisherman's refusal demonstrates the link through reasoning about the drought. This meets the top band.

sampleAnswers.answer: The fisherman refuses to sell his catch, which shows loyalty to the crew. The drought makes money hard to earn, so the economic context matters.
sampleAnswers.feedback: The perspective and a feature of the context are identified, but the answer does not reason about how the pressure shapes the perspective. This is the 2-mark band.

sampleAnswers.answer: The drought is a problem for the town and the people in it.
sampleAnswers.feedback: A general comment on the setting with no perspective named. This is the 1-mark standard.

prompts.scenario: A student is writing a short response on the same invented story, set in a fishing town during a drought. The response must demonstrate, using a specific episode, how one ethical perspective is shaped by economic pressure. The older fisherman refuses to sell his share of the catch, which the town's economy has made a matter of survival. When the boats cannot go out, the owners reduce wages.

dotPoints.description: The effect of theme and genre, and how these can influence a texts value

prompts.question: Evaluate the effect of theme and genre on a text's value.
markerNotes: Evaluate requires a judgement that is stated and then justified against the effects of theme and genre, not just a list of effects.
The strongest answers show when genre helps the theme and when it works against it, so the judgement is conditional and specific.
A closing sentence that repeats the rating is not a judgement; the criteria behind the rating must be stated.
commonStudentErrors: Describes the theme and the genre without deciding how much each adds to the value.
Gives a rating ('it is a 9 out of 10') with no criteria for the rating.
prompts.markingCriteria:
6 marks: Reaches a clear, sustained judgement on the effect of theme and genre on value, weighing both with relevant evidence
5 marks: Makes a judgement about theme and genre with a partial weighing of their effects
4 marks: Describes the effects of theme and genre and reaches a broad judgement
3 marks: Describes theme or genre with a general comment on value
2 marks: Makes a general statement about value with little evaluation
1 mark: Makes a relevant but unsupported comment

sampleAnswers.answer: The effect of theme and genre on a text's value is real but conditional, and an evaluation has to decide when each helps and when each limits. The invented thriller's theme, the corruption of a city's institutions, gives the work its moral weight, because the reader is invited to care about who is protected and who is sacrificed. A theme of this kind has value when it is developed through character and consequence rather than announced. Genre has a more complicated influence. The thriller's conventions, including the ticking clock, the reversal and the final confrontation, provide structure and momentum, and they reward readers who know the form. However, genre can also reduce a text's value when its conventions become formulas, so the reader expects the ending before it arrives. In this thriller the conventions are used with some restraint, and the theme gains force because the genre does not overwhelm it. My judgement is that the theme provides the text's lasting value while the genre provides the means of delivering it. The text is strongest when the two reinforce one another, and weakest where a predictable genre pattern replaces the theme. A reviewer who weighs both carefully will rate the thriller highly, though not for every reason the genre would suggest.
sampleAnswers.feedback: The answer states a conditional judgement on the value of theme and genre, weighs the influence of each against the other, and gives the criteria for the rating. This is the sustained evaluation the top band requires.

sampleAnswers.answer: The theme of corruption gives the thriller moral weight, and that is valuable. The genre also helps, because the ticking clock creates tension. However, some of the genre conventions are predictable, which lowers the value of the story a little. Overall the thriller is good and I would rate it highly.
sampleAnswers.feedback: The effects of theme and genre are described and a broad judgement is reached, but the criteria for that judgement are general and the weighing is brief. This is the 4-mark band.

sampleAnswers.answer: The thriller has a theme and a genre, which make it valuable.
sampleAnswers.feedback: A relevant comment with no evaluation of the effect of either element. This is the 1-mark standard.

prompts.scenario: A reviewer must decide whether an invented thriller, written for this task, deserves a high rating for its theme and its genre conventions. The review will be read by students who have not yet encountered the text, so the reviewer must weigh whether genre helps or limits the work's value. Its theme is the corruption of a city's institutions, and its conventions include a ticking clock, a reversal and a final confrontation.

prompts.question: Summarise how theme and genre together can determine the value a reader places on a text.
markerNotes: A summary must be shorter than the material it covers and must still state the main relationship. Length is not the measure.
The strongest answers state how the two elements interact, not just that each one matters.
Avoid introducing new evidence; the summary should draw on what is already known.
commonStudentErrors: Retells the plot of the thriller instead of summarising how theme and genre determine value.
Mentions theme and genre as two separate points with no statement of how they interact.
prompts.markingCriteria:
3 marks: Summarises accurately and concisely how theme and genre together determine value, and states the relationship between them
2 marks: Summarises the effect of theme or genre on value with limited detail
1 mark: Makes a relevant but general comment

sampleAnswers.answer: Theme and genre together determine the value a reader places on a text. Theme gives the work its moral or emotional weight, while genre shapes the reader's expectations and pleasures. When genre conventions carry the theme, the reader feels the value of both; when the genre becomes a formula, the theme is overshadowed and the value falls. The value of the text is therefore a product of the two working together.
sampleAnswers.feedback: The summary is concise, states how theme and genre determine value, and draws the relationship between them. This earns full marks.

sampleAnswers.answer: Theme gives a text moral weight and genre gives the reader expectations, so both affect how much a reader values it.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Both elements are linked to value, but the interaction is not stated and the summary has little detail. This is the 2-mark band.

sampleAnswers.answer: Theme and genre are both important to a text.
sampleAnswers.feedback: A general comment that does not summarise how either element determines value. This is the 1-mark standard.

prompts.scenario: A teacher is preparing a short revision summary on how theme and genre affect the value a reader places on a text, for students who are about to write an extended response on an invented thriller written for this task.

dotPoints.description: Compose critical texts that affirm or challenge the ideas, values and perspectives represented in a complex text

prompts.question: Construct a critical text that affirms or challenges the ideas, values and perspectives represented in the novel. Follow your text with a short rationale explaining your choices.
markerNotes: The composed text must take a position that is developed across the piece. Affirming in one paragraph and challenging in another is strong only if the two are linked by a clear argument.
The rationale should explain choices of form, register and evidence, and it should be consistent with the text. A rationale that describes a different text is marked down.
Marks reward control of the critical register: precise claims, evidence drawn from the complex text, and a judgement the reader can test.
commonStudentErrors: Writes a plot summary of the novel and adds a single sentence of opinion, so the text is not critical.
Writes a rationale that restates the composed text rather than explaining the choices made in it.
prompts.markingCriteria:
7-8 marks: Constructs a sustained critical text that affirms and challenges the ideas, values and perspectives of the complex text with control of form and register, and a rationale that explains specific choices
5-6 marks: Constructs a critical text that affirms or challenges the complex text with clear control of form, and a rationale that describes some choices
3-4 marks: Constructs a brief critical text with an uneven position, and a rationale that makes a general claim
1-2 marks: Constructs a text with a limited critical position and little or no rationale

sampleAnswers.answer:
Review: A Family Ledger Rewritten

The invented novel in this scenario presents inheritance as a debt that each generation must settle on its own terms, and its ideas about duty deserve critical affirmation. Yet the complex text is most powerful when it resists its own moral certainties. Its values are presented through a narrator who insists that loyalty to the family is the highest good, and the novel asks the reader to share that conviction for most of its length. Affirmation lies in the way the book makes this loyalty costly. Each sacrifice made for the family is recorded with a precision that holds the reader's sympathy, and the perspectives of the younger characters surface in small, unresolved ways that gather weight. Challenge emerges in the final chapters, where the narrator's ledger is revealed to be incomplete. The novel does not condemn loyalty; it asks whether the family's ideas about it have been applied to some members and not others. A critical reader cannot leave the book with the narrator's values intact. The complex text thus affirms duty as a value worth dignifying while challenging the perspective that duty alone justifies its cost. That tension is the novel's achievement, and it is why the work rewards the reader willing to disagree with it.

Rationale: I chose the review form because it allows a critical voice to affirm the novel's ideas about duty while disputing its values. The register is measured and evaluative, matching a literary magazine's readers. I used the narrator's ledger as the controlling image so that affirmation and challenge arise from the same textual detail. The closing sentence returns to tension to leave the reader with an open judgement, which is the perspective the review models.
sampleAnswers.feedback: The composed review holds a developed critical position: it affirms the ideas about duty and challenges the values behind them, using one controlling image throughout. The rationale names specific choices (form, register, the ledger) and matches the text, so it earns full marks.

sampleAnswers.answer:
Review: The ideas about family duty in this novel are strong, and the narrator's loyalty is admirable. However, the novel challenges some values, because the younger characters suffer for the family's sake. The complex text makes the reader think about whether duty is always right, and I think it is worth reading for that reason.

Rationale: I wrote this as a review because it is a critical form, and I wanted to say both what the novel does well and where it goes wrong.
sampleAnswers.feedback: The composed text takes a position that affirms and challenges, but the two are placed side by side rather than argued, and the rationale describes the form without explaining choices of evidence. This sits in the 5-6 band.

sampleAnswers.answer:
The novel is about a family and their duty. It affirms some values and challenges others.

Rationale: I wrote a review.
sampleAnswers.feedback: A limited critical position and a rationale that does not explain any choice. This is the 1-2 mark band at its upper end.

prompts.scenario: A literary magazine invites students to contribute a critical review of the invented complex text in this scenario, a multi-layered novel about a family's inheritance, written for this task. Contributions must argue whether the novel's ideas about duty deserve affirmation or challenge. Its narrator keeps a ledger recording each family sacrifice, and insists that loyalty is the highest good. Its younger characters' perspectives surface in small ways, and in its final chapters the ledger is revealed to be incomplete.

prompts.question: Explain how a critical response can challenge the values represented in a complex text, using ONE technique from the novel.
markerNotes: Explain requires a mechanism. A strong answer shows how a technique in the complex text carries the value, and how a critical reading turns that technique against it.
One technique is enough if it is developed. A list of three techniques, each brief, is weaker than one technique explained in full.
Avoid asserting that a value is wrong without showing the textual basis for the claim.
commonStudentErrors: States that the novel's values are wrong without identifying a technique that carries them.
Names a technique such as 'imagery' but does not show how it supports the value being challenged.
prompts.markingCriteria:
