sampleAnswers.answer:
Still, I carried the box up the stairs as though it held something that might bite. Forty years of my grandfather’s letters lay inside, tied with string gone the colour of old tobacco, and I had been promised that they would explain him. I sat on the landing and untied the first bundle. The letters were courteous. They asked after the weather, the price of wool and the health of a sister in the hills. They thanked a neighbour for a jar of plums. Nowhere did they say what had happened on the night the telephone rang and he went out without his coat.

I read them the way you read someone else’s post, guiltily and too quickly, and by the third bundle I understood the trick. Every sentence was a lid. Each one closed over whatever it meant to hide, the way a sheet is drawn over a table nobody has yet cleared. Words and ideas, the careful drafts of a man who would not be seen. Dry and dead as dust, yes. But dust settles on whatever is left in a room, and I had begun to notice what was left.

At the bottom of the box, under a tin of tacks and a mouth organ with two notes missing, lay a child’s exercise book. Its cover had been coloured in with crayon: a blue sky, a yellow house, a figure in the doorway with both arms stretched wide. Inside, a boy had copied one sentence eleven times. I will come back before the rain. Each copy leaned further than the last, the letters running downhill as if the pencil were hurrying to finish before someone called him in for tea. Nobody had written down what he was afraid of. The pages did the telling in the only language a child truly commands, which is repetition.

I had come to read a man and was reading a house. The mouth organ had been played until its brass went soft at the edges; someone had pressed a thumb into it every night, the way you test a bruise. The tacks were the kind used for mending lino or hanging a picture in a hall. The exercise book had been kept, not thrown out, and that was the secret of it. A person does not keep what means nothing. They keep whatever would hurt more to lose.

Outside, a magpie began its long and uncertain song. The boy at the table, I realised, had been my grandfather, writing the same sentence until it was true. I wanted to tell him that he had written his letters too politely to be understood. The real account of his life was not in what he had said but in what he had carried up and down the same stairs for forty years: the tacks, the mouth organ, a small promise kept in pencil and then in a box.

I set the exercise book on top of the pile and the letters underneath it, so that the boy would be read first. Then I went down to the kitchen to make tea, the way my grandmother did whenever news had arrived that nobody could yet bear to say aloud. The kettle ticked as it cooled. I thought about the things I would leave behind, the receipts and recipes and half-finished crosswords, and about the strange hope that someone might one day sit on a landing with my shoebox and find me not in the words but in the stubborn small evidence of having been here.

Dust is what remains when everything has been said. I had mistaken it for the end of the story. It is only the place where the story waits for a reader willing to kneel down and look under the furniture.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 17-20 mark row: the piece composes a sustained and engaging continuation that moves from the courteous letters to the child’s book, and it crafts language skilfully so that the reader reaches the grandfather’s boyhood before the narrator names it. The move that would lift it is to cut the sentence beginning “Dust is what remains”, since the room and the furniture already carry the idea.

sampleAnswers.answer:
Still, I took the box upstairs and sat on the bed with it, because the letters were what I had come for. Forty years of my grandfather’s correspondence lay inside, tied in bundles with string. I expected the letters to explain him. They did not. They were polite and careful, about the weather, the price of wool and a sister who had moved to the coast. They thanked people for small kindnesses. I read through three bundles and felt that I had learned nothing new about the man I thought I knew.

Then I found the rest of the box, at the bottom, under the letters. It held a tin of tacks, a mouth organ and an exercise book with a blue cover. The book had been coloured in by a child. Inside, a boy had written the same sentence over and over: I will come back before the rain. The handwriting got worse with each copy, and by the end the letters were sloping down the page. I realised that nobody had told the child what to say. He had decided it himself, and he had kept repeating it until he believed it.

I thought about how easily the things we leave behind can be misread. A letter is written for a reader, so it shows the face a person wants to show. A mouth organ is only what it is. Someone had played it every night until the brass wore soft, and that wear was more honest than anything my grandfather had written down. The tacks had been kept too, in a tin that rattled whenever the box was moved.

I put the book on top of the letters and went downstairs. The kettle was already on and the kitchen smelled of the plums in the jar. I could not stop thinking about the boy, or about the sentence he had copied so many times. Perhaps it had been true. Perhaps the man who kept it had needed one promise to hold on to, and the rest of his life had been a long wait for it to come back.

Words are not the only record of a life. The things we keep, even dull things like tacks, tell a reader where a person’s attention went. I had come to the box to find a man. I found a house, and a child in it, and I began to understand that the secret had never been in the letters at all.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 9-12 mark row: the piece composes a sound continuation that moves from the letters to the child’s book, and its language is competent, though the last paragraph restates the opening idea (words are not the only record of a life) rather than extending it. To reach 13, carry the image of the child’s book through to the end, so that the reader reaches the conclusion without its being stated.

sampleAnswers.answer: I opened the box and the letters were all about the weather and the price of wool. They did not say much about him, and I could not tell which of them mattered. The box was heavier than I expected, and the string had rotted at the knots. Then I found a book that a boy had written in, and it said I will come back before the rain many times. I felt sad for the boy. I think things tell you more than words do, because people write what they want you to read. The kitchen clock was loud, and the tea took a long time to brew. I put the book on top and went downstairs.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 5-8 mark row: the piece attempts to continue the extract simply, moving from the letters to the child’s book, but the language shifts between plain statement and an abstract claim (I think things tell you more than words do), and no image is developed. To reach 9, follow one object from the box through the paragraph so that the reader sees the boy rather than being told about him.

prompts.question: Use the image provided to craft a central metaphor in a piece of imaginative, discursive or persuasive writing.
markerNotes: A central metaphor has to run through the whole piece. The marker looks for an image that is returned to and developed, not one that appears once and is dropped.
The stimulus should do work in the writing: look for how the image shapes the situation, the language and the ending.
A persuasive or discursive piece can state a view, but the view should arise from the metaphor rather than sit beside it.
Control of language shows in image choice and sentence rhythm. A metaphor explained in a sentence of comment loses its effect.
commonStudentErrors: Describing what is in the image without developing it into a metaphor for an idea.
Introducing a metaphor and then explaining it, so the reader is told the meaning instead of shown it.
Mixing images from different ideas, so that the central metaphor is lost.
Treating the stimulus as a starting point, then dropping it for an unrelated story.

sampleAnswers.answer:
The gate is locked at six, so I have stopped waiting for it. My hand comes through the chain-link first, then my wrist, then the pencil I sharpened on the concrete step, a stub of yellow wood with a point worn to a grey tooth. I lay the paper flat in the dirt below the wire and begin. The first footprint is narrow and deliberate, the shoe of someone who has decided not to look back. The second lands further on, in the long grass where the fence throws its shadow in diamonds. Each line I draw is a step I am allowed to take.

People tell me a fence is a fence. They point at the wire and the padlock and the bins behind the bus shelter, and they are right about everything except the paper. Paper has no gate. A footprint pressed into it does not ask permission to leave the car park or the concrete yard where the boys in bright jackets wait. It simply goes. By the time the sun has moved over the bitumen, the trail has reached the tree line, and I can see the path bending round the hill as clearly as if a surveyor had marked it with string.

Here is what I want you to understand. A road is only a line that enough feet have agreed to trust. Somebody walked the first one, and then somebody else walked it, until the council paved it and the route seemed inevitable. I am starting that trust again, with a pencil and a scrap of paper and a hand that has grown tired of holding onto wire. Draw the way out before you try to climb. The paper will carry you further than the fence was ever built to allow.

The fence will still be here tomorrow, and the padlock will still hang on the gate. But the footprints are already walking, and a body that walks is much harder to lock in than a body that waits. I ease my hand back through the wire, the way you draw a thread out of a knot. The pencil stays on the paper a moment longer. Then I follow the trail I have made.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 9-10 mark row: the piece composes a highly engaging piece of writing that uses the stimulus as a central metaphor, with the footprints becoming a road and the final image returning the walking to the hand in the fence, and control of language holds across all four paragraphs. The move that would lift it is to cut the sentence “Here is what I want you to understand.”, which announces the metaphor before the image has finished working.

sampleAnswers.answer:
The fence is high and the gate is locked, so I draw a way out instead. My hand goes through the wire and the pencil makes footprints on the paper underneath. Each footprint is a step. If I keep drawing, the footprints go all the way to the trees, and that is like a road. A road is a line that people walk on, so I am making one. The fence cannot stop a drawing. People say you cannot get out of a place like this, but I think you can if you draw it first.

The pencil is my leg and the paper is the field. I press the wire down with my other hand so the paper does not slip. The grass is wet and cold on my knees, and every footprint I draw is a little more certain than the one before. Behind me the bus rattles past and the wire hums, and I do not look round. I do not need the gate. I need the paper to be big enough and the footprints to look as if they know where they are going. When I pull my hand back through the fence, the trail is still there, and I can follow it. That is the only way I have got out so far.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 5-6 mark row: the piece uses the stimulus as a metaphor and keeps the footprints walking away from the fence, but the metaphor is explained in sentences of comment (that is like a road; that is the only way) rather than carried by the image, and several sentences open in the same pattern. To reach 7, let the footprints do the explaining in the description and cut the comment.

sampleAnswers.answer: I can see a fence and a hand holding a pencil. The pencil has drawn footprints on the paper under the fence. The fence is metal and it is high, so the person cannot get out. The footprints go away from the fence. I think drawing is a useful way to escape because you can go anywhere on paper. The footprints are the important part, and they show the person is leaving the place they are stuck in. The paper is on the ground, and the hand is still in the fence, so the drawing is the only thing that moves. The fence is cold, and the person looks tired.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 3-4 mark row: the piece attempts to respond to the stimulus and names the fence, the hand and the footprints, but the metaphor is announced (I think drawing is a useful way to escape) rather than developed, and the control of language is variable. To reach 5, let the footprints stand for the escape within the description itself, without comment.

prompts.question: Craft an imaginative or discursive piece of writing that explores a shared experience which brings about a sense of fulfilment.
markerNotes: The question asks for a shared experience on the page. Other people should be doing something with the narrator from the first paragraph, not only appearing in her memory of the night.
Fulfilment should be built through action, dialogue and a changing atmosphere. A closing line announcing that the experience was fulfilling tells the marker what the writing should have shown.
Control shows in shifts of sentence length and in imagery carried through the whole piece rather than dropped after one sentence.
A discursive form such as a speech, letter or reflection is acceptable if the form is controlled throughout. A change of form or point of view in the middle of the piece reads as a loss of control.
commonStudentErrors: Listing the events of a gathering, such as the food and the games, without one moment the reader can hold.
Stating how the group felt in general terms, rather than building the feeling through what people do and say.
Shifting the focus to the narrator alone in the last paragraph, so the shared experience is lost.
Ending on the abstract idea of fulfilment rather than on a concrete image that carries it.

sampleAnswers.answer:
The power went at six, somewhere between the first crack of thunder and the second, and by seven the whole street had come out to stare at the dark. Nobody had a plan. Mrs Kovac from number four had a pot of soup she could not heat. Dev from across the road had a sack of potatoes he had been meaning to get rid of since winter. I had two bread rolls and a bottle of red I had been saving for a birthday I had forgotten to celebrate.

We built the fire in the cul-de-sac from the fence palings Dev had been stacking since spring. It caught slowly, then all at once, and the crack of it went across the wet bitumen like a second storm. Somebody dragged out the patio chairs. Somebody else found a camp stove and two saucepans that did not match. By eight there was a ring of us, twelve people perhaps, holding paper plates on our knees and not quite looking at one another, the way neighbours do when they have never needed anything from each other.

Food changed that. Mrs Kovac’s soup was thin and salty and too hot to eat, and she stood over the pot with a wooden spoon, refusing help, until the children were fed first. Dev’s potatoes went into the coals wrapped in foil, and we burned our fingers pulling them out. The bread was torn rather than sliced. Nobody said grace, but everybody waited for the first mouthful, and when it was the youngest boy who got it, the whole circle laughed as if somebody had told a joke.

I had not planned to speak. I have spent most of my life in other people’s stories, the quiet one at the edge of the room who is good at listening. But the stories began to come by themselves. Dev’s father had once rowed a borrowed boat across a lake in a storm and come home with the oars bent. Mrs Kovac, silent through the soup, told us about a winter when the snow rose to the windowsills and the whole street shared one radio. When my turn came I told them about my grandmother’s kitchen, which had no power either, and how she lit the stove with newspaper and read aloud by its glow. My voice shook. Nobody interrupted. The fire took each story and gave it back to us warmer.

Somewhere after ten the flames sank to a low orange breath, and we moved closer without anybody suggesting it. Knees touched. A child fell asleep against Dev’s shoulder and he did not shift for an hour. The talk slowed into something like music: long pauses, then a laugh that started in the middle of a sentence and rolled around the circle. I felt something loosen in my chest, something I had been holding since the funeral in March, and I let it go without deciding to.

At eleven the power came back. The street lamps flickered on one by one, a fridge hummed in number six, and a television blared behind a closed door. Nobody got up. A small girl asked whether the fire could stay on until morning, and nobody had the heart to say no. Mrs Kovac rolled her eyes at the lights, then turned back to the coals. ‘Well,’ said Dev, in the voice that meant not yet. I pulled the blanket from the back of my chair and tucked it around my knees. The embers settled to grey. The street stayed lit, and we stayed where we were.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 13-15 mark row: the piece composes a highly engaging piece of imaginative writing that effectively responds to the question. It crafts language skilfully to explore a shared experience that brings about a sense of fulfilment, building the feeling through the food, the stories and the closeness of the circle rather than announcing it. It demonstrates highly effective control of language and structure appropriate to audience, purpose, context and selected form, with the power returning at the end to close the arc.

sampleAnswers.answer:
The four of us had driven down to the coast on the last weekend of the year, and by the second night we had run out of things to say to each other. Tom had brought a guitar but only knew two chords. Priya had brought enough food for a wedding. I had brought a camera I never used. We had been friends since high school and somewhere along the way we had become polite.

Then the fire went up. We had gathered driftwood from the dunes, and when Tom struck the match the flames shot higher than any of us expected and we all jumped back, laughing. After that it was easy. We cooked sausages on a grill that Priya had borrowed from her uncle, burned half of them, and ate the rest with our fingers. The sand was cold and the air was warm, and the sea kept coming in behind us.

Priya told the story about her grandmother’s garden. Tom admitted he had cried at a film the week before. I talked about the year I moved away and came home again, and how strange it felt to be back. We listened to each other properly for the first time in months. It felt like a gift that nobody had asked for.

As the fire burned down we sat close together and watched the sparks climb into the dark. I felt complete. It was the best night I could remember, and I did not want it to end. I felt grateful for these people and for the chance to be together somewhere with no phone signal and no work.

When the coals went grey we walked back up the dunes in the dark, our torches swinging. Tom was still humming his two chords. We knew it was the start of a new year, and we knew we would be different because of what we had shared.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 7-9 mark row: the piece composes an imaginative piece that responds to the question and uses language competently to explore a shared experience among friends at the coast. It demonstrates sound control of language and structure appropriate to selected form. To reach 10, build the sense of fulfilment through action and dialogue rather than stating it: the closing paragraphs tell the reader the night was complete, and the sparks appear once and are not carried through the piece.

sampleAnswers.answer: We went down to the beach for a fire with some friends. We had food, and we cooked sausages and marshmallows. Everyone was there and it was nice. We talked about school and the holidays and what we were going to do next year. The sand was cold and somebody played music on a phone. I got sausage on my shirt and everyone laughed at me about it. Then the fire went out and we went home. It is a good night and I feel happy about being with my friends. It was a nice time and we were all very relaxed. Sharing food and stories with people is important, and I think everyone needs that.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 4-6 mark row: the piece attempts to respond to the question, naming a gathering at the beach without developing it, and it demonstrates variable control of language and structure, since the tense moves from past to present in the closing sentences. To reach 7, render the gathering through specific moments and detail, and keep the tense and the point of view stable.

prompts.scenario:
Stimulus: ‘Her mind wandered. Last night had been something. Alive. Yes. She had felt alive. Kindled. Lit. Blazing. She had forgotten the way being around other people could feel . . . The sharing of food. The sharing of stories. The gathering around a fire. Elemental. And no one had required anything of her. She had been allowed to just listen. To absorb. She’d forgotten how much she was capable of absorbing.’ — Vanessa McCausland, The Beautiful Words

prompts.hscSection: Paper 2, Section III — Module C: The Craft of Writing (20 marks). Allow about 40 minutes.

prompts.question: Use this extract as the stimulus for an imaginative or discursive piece of writing that explores the hope that comes with anticipation.
markerNotes: The question asks for the hope that comes with anticipation, so the strongest pieces make the reader wait with the narrator. Hope needs a future that is still uncertain, and the piece should keep that future open until its last lines.

The stimulus gives a sound, a time of night and a line about morning. Strong pieces let those details govern the structure, rather than using them as decoration on a story that could have been written about anything.
Control shows when the story moves from night to morning in stages the reader can follow, and when the sentence rhythm changes as the mood lifts.
A piece that tells the reader it is hopeful, or lists what the narrator is excited about, names the feeling without earning it. Show the anticipation through action and small detail.
commonStudentErrors: Stating that the narrator is hopeful or excited without showing the waiting that produces the feeling.
Using the bird’s song once and then dropping it, so the stimulus does not shape the piece.
Confusing hope with happiness, so the piece celebrates an outcome that has already arrived rather than one still to come.
Shifting between tenses or points of view, which weakens the sense of a single moment held in suspense.
prompts.markingCriteria:
10-12 marks: Composes a highly engaging piece of writing that skilfully uses the stimulus; Crafts language skilfully to compose a piece of writing that explores the hope that comes with anticipation; Demonstrates highly effective control of language and structure appropriate to audience, purpose, context and selected form
7-9 marks: Composes an engaging piece of writing that uses the stimulus; Crafts language effectively to compose a piece of writing that explores the hope that comes with anticipation; Demonstrates effective control of language and structure appropriate to audience, purpose, context and selected form
4-6 marks: Composes a piece of writing that adequately uses the stimulus; Uses language adequately to compose a piece of writing; Demonstrates variable control of language and structure appropriate to audience, purpose, context and selected form
1-3 marks: Attempts to compose a piece of writing that has some relevance to the question; Demonstrates limited control of language

sampleAnswers.answer:
The bird starts at four. I know it is four because the clock on my bedside table has just turned from 3:59 to 4:00 in its pale green light, and because the first notes come through the open window the way they always do: one, two, three, four, then a silence long enough for me to wonder whether I dreamed them. I did not dream them. Somewhere in the gum tree beyond the back fence, a small bird is telling the street that the night is nearly finished.

Mum comes home today. For six weeks the word home has belonged to a ward with a window that looks onto a car park, and now it belongs to this house: the kitchen where the kettle clicks, the hallway where her slippers wait under the coat hooks. The doctors have finally given us a time, ten o’clock, after the morning round and the paperwork. I have been awake since two, rehearsing the day the way you rehearse a speech. Sheets on the line. Soup in the pot. The armchair turned to face the garden.

I count the notes with my fingers under the blanket. One for the kettle, two for the bread, three for the car door, four for the moment she walks through the gate and does not need my arm on the step. It is a silly game, I know. But anticipation is like that. It cuts a long wait into small handholds, each one a little more solid than the last.

Fear arrives all at once, with a phone call or a shadow across the ceiling. Hope is slower. It builds the way the light builds in the corners of the room, one thread at a time, until the wardrobe door shows its crack of brightness and the cup on the sill comes into focus.

Dad rang last night to say the nurses had found her walking the corridor with her cardigan buttoned wrong, asking for the bus home. He laughed when he told me, and so did I. It was the first laugh in weeks that sounded like the old house.

The bird sings again, and this time I answer it, not aloud, only in the small voice I keep for things that might be listening. All is well, I think. Morning is coming. Then the street begins to wake: a car turns over two doors down, a dog barks once and thinks better of it, and the sky above the fence loosens from grey into a thin blue that promises a warm day.

At half past six I open the window wider and let in the cold, the wet grass and somebody’s wood smoke. The bird is still going, slower now, as though it has decided its work is done. I make two cups of tea. Then, because the day is too full to stand still, I make a third and carry it upstairs to the room where she will sleep tonight. I set it on the sill and watch the steam climb into the light.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 10-12 mark row: the piece composes a highly engaging piece of writing that skilfully uses the stimulus, and crafts language skilfully to explore the hope that comes with anticipation. The four-note song is counted out as a daily rhythm and the light builds slowly, so the waiting is held open until the final paragraph. It demonstrates highly effective control of language and structure appropriate to audience, purpose, context and selected form.

sampleAnswers.answer:
I wake at four because a bird is singing. It is a small bird and it sings four notes at a time, then stops. I lie there and listen to it. I know Mum comes home today, which is why I am awake, and I feel happy and nervous at the same time.

The doctors said she could come home today. We have been waiting for six weeks. I have cleaned the house twice and bought the biscuits she likes, the ones with the chocolate on the bottom. I want everything to be right when she arrives. I think she will be pleased, but I am not sure.

I hear the bird again and it makes me hopeful. I think the bird is saying that morning is coming and everything will be all right. I did not expect to feel so calm, but I suppose waiting makes you hopeful. Dad rang last night and said Mum was getting better every day. This made me very happy.

The sky gets lighter. The street wakes up. A car starts two doors down and a dog barks. I make a cup of tea and drink it at the kitchen table, looking out at the garden. It is going to be a nice day. I can feel something good is about to happen, and I am excited about it.

By ten o’clock Mum will be here, and the house will feel like a home again. I hope she likes the chair I turned to face the garden. The bird has stopped singing now. I think it is finished too.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 7-9 mark row: the piece composes an engaging piece of writing that uses the stimulus, and crafts language effectively to explore the hope that comes with anticipation. The song frames the opening and closing, but the narrator names her feelings directly (happy and nervous, very happy, excited) and the middle paragraphs are organised as a sequence of events. To reach 10, replace each stated feeling with a detail of the waiting and keep the song shaping the middle of the piece.

sampleAnswers.answer: This is about a girl who is waiting for her mum to come home from hospital. It is early in the morning and there is a bird singing outside the window. She is happy because her mum is coming back and she has made tea. The bird sings four notes and then it stops. Hope is a good feeling to have when you are waiting for something. The girl is hopeful that everything will be alright and she is going to see her mum soon. She has cleaned the house and bought biscuits. In the end the sun comes up and the day starts, and that is the end of the story.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 1-3 mark row: the piece attempts to compose a piece of writing with some relevance to the question, and demonstrates limited control of language. It retells events in order and states the hope in general terms rather than showing the anticipation. To reach 4, use the stimulus to organise the waiting, with the bird’s song setting the time, and show the hope through what the narrator does.

prompts.scenario:
Stimulus: ‘In the middle of the night, around four am, sometimes/often/but not always, a bird sings a four-note song at intervals. It doesn’t wake me up but when I lie there I hear it and imagine it is letting all the other birds and the rest of us know that all is well. Morning is coming.’ — Stephanie Radok, Under the Bed

prompts.hscSection: Paper 2, Section III — Module C: The Craft of Writing (20 marks). Allow about 40 minutes.

prompts.question: Craft an imaginative piece of writing which incorporates the provided image as the focus of your narrative.
markerNotes: The image has to be the focus of the narrative, not a backdrop. The strongest pieces let the story turn on what the image shows, such as the people who stand before it and the light that passes through it.

Use the specific features of the stimulus: the round glass face, the Roman numerals, the crossed frame, the silhouettes and the light. A piece that only mentions a clock could be written about any image.
Control shows when the image returns at the end with a changed meaning, rather than appearing as a list of details in the opening paragraph.
Describe the silhouettes and the light through the narrator’s experience of them. A description written like a caption for the photograph keeps the image outside the story.
commonStudentErrors: Describing the photograph as a flat inventory of details, so the image sits beside the story instead of driving it.
Using the clock as a general symbol of time passing, with no particular moment or consequence in the plot.
Writing a story with no connection between the figures in silhouette and the narrator.
Ignoring the light that floods through the glass, so the piece loses the contrast between light and shadow that the image depends on.
prompts.markingCriteria:
10-12 marks: Composes a highly engaging piece of writing that skilfully incorporates the image as the focus of the narrative; Crafts language skilfully to compose a piece of writing that incorporates the image as the focus of the narrative; Demonstrates highly effective control of language and structure appropriate to audience, purpose, context and narrative form
7-9 marks: Composes an engaging piece of writing that uses the image as the focus of the narrative; Crafts language effectively to compose a piece of writing that incorporates the image as the focus of the narrative; Demonstrates effective control of language and structure appropriate to audience, purpose, context and narrative form
4-6 marks: Composes a piece of writing that adequately uses the image; Uses language adequately to compose a piece of writing; Demonstrates variable control of language and structure appropriate to audience, purpose, context and form
1-3 marks: Attempts to compose a piece of writing that has some relevance to the question; Demonstrates limited control of language

sampleAnswers.answer:
Everyone under the clock is a silhouette. I notice this before the timetable, before the cold, before the boy with the skateboard who keeps circling the pillar. The morning light pours through the great round face of glass, so the people waiting beneath it are turned to shadow, each one cut flat against the brightness. Roman numerals burn at the edge of the light. A crossed frame divides the face into quarters, and the people nearest the centre look like figures trapped inside a window.

I told Dad to meet me here. Under the clock, I said, the way Mum used to say when I was small and wandering off in the crowd. It has been four years since I heard his voice properly. Four years since the phone calls stopped and the birthday cards began arriving late, with stamps that do not match the postmarks. I have rehearsed what I will say. Now the rehearsed words have gone, and I am holding the ticket in my hand as if it might be evidence.

The hour is close. I can feel it in the crowd, the small shifts as people check their watches and then lift their faces to the glass, as though the clock were a promise it must keep. The minute hand moves. The shadows slide across the stone floor and reshape themselves. A man in a long coat steps into the light and becomes only a shape. A woman with a pram stops. A boy swings his bag in a slow circle, and his shadow swings with him, bigger and blacker than the boy himself.

I want to step forward and be part of it. Instead I stay where I am, one foot in the glare and one in the cool shade of the pillar, and I watch the silhouettes the way I would watch a film I have already seen: knowing the ending, hoping it might change.

Then one figure separates from the rest. It walks out from beneath the clock with its hands pushed into its pockets, unhurried, as though it has walked this path a thousand times. Its outline is too thin at the shoulders and too straight at the back. It stops two metres away, with the light behind it, and I can see nothing of its face at all.

‘Ruby?’

The voice is lower than I remember and rougher at the edges. It is the only thing in this whole building I am sure of. I take the step I could not take a moment ago, and the light slides off his face and onto mine. Above us the great glass face ticks over into the next minute, and for the first time all morning, we are both standing in the light.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 10-12 mark row: the piece composes a highly engaging piece of writing that skilfully incorporates the image as the focus of the narrative. It crafts language skilfully, with the silhouettes, the Roman numerals, the crossed frame and the light all working in the plot, and it demonstrates highly effective control of language and structure appropriate to audience, purpose, context and narrative form. The return to the image in the final paragraph changes its meaning, from a meeting point to a moment of recognition.

sampleAnswers.answer:
The clock in the station is huge and made of glass, with Roman numerals around its edge. I am meeting my dad under it for the first time in years. I got here early and I stand near the pillar, watching the crowd. People are standing in front of the clock and they look like shadows because the light is coming through the glass. It is very bright.

I feel nervous. The last time I saw Dad I was eleven and he was leaving for work. Mum said he would come back when he was ready. I do not know what he will say. I hope he is different now and I hope I am too.

The minute hand goes round. A man in a coat walks past and his shape is black against the light. A woman with a pram waits by the bench. A boy is swinging his bag, and it makes a shadow on the floor that is bigger than him. Everybody is looking at the clock because it is nearly time.

Then a figure comes out from under the clock. It is a man, but I cannot see his face because of the light behind him. He stops in front of me and says my name. I feel relief and fear at the same time. The light moves and now I can see him, and it is Dad, and he looks older than I thought. We stand under the clock and everything feels different now, like a new start.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 7-9 mark row: the piece composes an engaging piece of writing that uses the image as the focus of the narrative, and crafts language effectively, though the clock is often the setting rather than a driver of the plot. The narrator names her feelings (nervous, relief and fear, everything feels different), and the closing lines summarise the meaning. To reach 10, let the image do the work in the final paragraph and cut the statements of feeling.

sampleAnswers.answer: There is a big clock in a station and people are standing under it. It is made of glass and it has numbers on it. The light comes through the glass and makes the people look dark. I am waiting for somebody. The clock says it is nearly ten o’clock. I am looking at the people and wondering who they are. A lot of people are here today, and the clock is a nice place to meet because everyone can see it. There are lots of people in the station and it is very busy. Some of them are standing still and some of them are walking. The shadows are long on the floor. I hope the person I am waiting for comes soon.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Meets the 1-3 mark row: the piece attempts to compose a piece of writing with some relevance to the question, and demonstrates limited control of language. It lists what is visible in the photograph without a narrative in which the image matters. To reach 4, give the narrator a problem under the clock and show what the silhouettes mean to her.

prompts.scenario:
Stimulus: a black-and-white photograph looking out through a huge round clock face of glass, with Roman numerals and a crossed frame; people stand in silhouette before it, with light flooding through.
